one_line: Leaderboard rank stability is governed by a single dimensionless quantity (score gap over sampling noise), yielding a precomputable 'minimum detectable delta' for any benchmark.
problem: Benchmarks report point scores without any principled statement of how large a score difference must be before a rank claim is meaningful for that specific test set.
core_hypothesis: Across heterogeneous benchmarks, the probability that a leaderboard rank flips under test-set resampling collapses onto one universal curve when plotted against the gap between two models divided by the standard error of the paired score difference.
falsifiable_prediction: Bootstrap resampling of many public benchmarks' per-item results will show rank-flip probability as a function of normalized gap falling on a single sigmoid within tight tolerance, regardless of task, metric, or modality.
why_important: A universal stability law would let any benchmark publish its minimum detectable delta at release time, converting leaderboard reading from folklore into measurement.
why_possibly_novel: Statistical significance of individual comparisons is often discussed, but a cross-benchmark collapse onto a single normalized stability curve, usable as a design rule, does not appear to be an established result (hypothesis; not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect per-item outputs for the top ~20 submissions on 5-10 benchmarks with public prediction files; bootstrap test sets; plot rank-flip rate against normalized gap per benchmark pair; test curve collapse with a goodness-of-fit criterion against the pooled curve.
main_risk: Heavy inter-item correlation (duplicates, shared sources) may make the effective sample size benchmark-specific, breaking the collapse unless correlation is estimated and folded into the normalization.
community_default_belief: Whether a leaderboard difference is trustworthy must be judged case by case, using ad hoc significance tests when authors bother.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Rank stability may be a purely statistical phenomenon determined by gap-to-noise ratio, in which case one calibration curve serves all benchmarks and case-by-case judgment is unnecessary.
fastest_falsification: If normalized rank-flip curves for even two large benchmarks differ grossly after correlation correction, there is no universal law.

one_line: A systematic census will show a large fraction of recent claimed SOTA improvements fall inside the same-method seed-variance band, with the fraction predictable from test-set size.
problem: Papers claim improvements over prior SOTA without reporting the run-to-run variance of their own method, so the field cannot tell progress from lottery.
core_hypothesis: For a substantial share of recent leaderboard deltas, re-running the identical baseline with different seeds spans the claimed improvement, and this share grows predictably as test-set size shrinks.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-running matched baselines with 5-10 seeds across a stratified sample of published comparisons will show the claimed delta within the baseline's seed band in a large minority of cases, with incidence inversely related to test-set size.
why_important: Quantifying how much of the literature's claimed progress is seed noise, and tying it to a controllable benchmark property (test size), turns a familiar complaint into an actionable design constraint.
why_possibly_novel: Seed-variance critiques exist for specific subfields; a cross-domain census that regresses 'delta inside noise band' incidence on benchmark size, enabling per-benchmark noise budgets, is hypothesized to be missing (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select ~30 published comparisons across 3 domains where code is available; rerun baseline with multiple seeds under the paper's protocol; record whether claimed deltas exceed the empirical seed band; regress incidence on test-set size.
main_risk: Reproduction fidelity: differences in environment or hyperparameters could inflate apparent seed variance and unfairly indict real improvements.
community_default_belief: A method that tops the leaderboard is better than the method below it.
why_that_may_be_wrong: When run-to-run variance exceeds the gap, top position is exchangeable under reruns, and the ordering is an artifact of publication selection on lucky seeds.
fastest_falsification: If reruns show seed bands are consistently much narrower than published deltas across the sample, the debunk fails.

one_line: Paired per-item evaluation exploits inter-model error correlation to certify leaderboard winners with several-fold fewer test items than unpaired scoring.
problem: Benchmarks size their test sets for absolute score estimation, but the community's actual use case is pairwise model comparison, which has different and usually cheaper statistical requirements.
core_hypothesis: Because strong models err on overlapping item subsets, paired-difference tests certify the same winner as full evaluation using a small fraction of items, with the savings factor an increasing function of inter-model error correlation.
falsifiable_prediction: On benchmarks with public per-item predictions, paired tests on random item subsets will reach the full-test-set verdict with the predicted item budget (derived from measured error correlation), while unpaired tests at the same budget stay inconclusive.
why_important: If pairwise certification is cheap, benchmarks can be smaller, refreshed more often, and partially held private, directly mitigating saturation and contamination.
why_possibly_novel: Paired statistics are standard in other measurement sciences, but a benchmark-design rule that sizes test sets from anticipated inter-model correlation is hypothesized to be unformalized in ML evaluation practice (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take per-item results for model pairs on 3 benchmarks; compute error correlations; subsample items at various budgets; compare verdict agreement rates of paired vs unpaired tests against the correlation-derived budget formula.
main_risk: Error correlation varies by model-pair similarity, so the budget rule may need pair-specific estimates, complicating the protocol it aims to simplify.
community_default_belief: Reliable evaluation requires large test sets; small test sets are inherently untrustworthy.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Reliability requirements depend on the question asked; for paired comparisons between correlated models, small samples can carry sufficient information.
fastest_falsification: If verdict agreement at the formula's budget is no better than unpaired testing on the first benchmark tried, the design rule fails.

one_line: Per-item error correlation between top submissions rises monotonically with benchmark age as models converge on shared training corpora and recipes.
problem: Benchmarks are treated as static instruments, but the statistical relationship among the models they measure changes over time, altering what a score difference means.
core_hypothesis: As a benchmark ages, surviving submissions become increasingly correlated in their per-item errors, so late-era rank distinctions are statistically easier (paired noise shrinks) but reflect ever-narrower behavioral differences.
falsifiable_prediction: For leaderboards with archived per-item predictions, the mean pairwise error correlation of the top decile of submissions will increase across submission-date cohorts, and the paired standard error of top-pair comparisons will shrink faster than the score gaps do.
why_important: The finding would recalibrate how late-benchmark-life 'wins' should be read: precise but behaviorally tiny, which matters for deployment decisions premised on leaderboard deltas.
why_possibly_novel: Benchmark aging is usually discussed as saturation of scores; aging of the error-correlation structure, and its consequence for what rank differences mean, is hypothesized to be unexamined (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Harvest archived per-item prediction files from 2-3 long-lived leaderboards; compute pairwise error correlations within submission cohorts; fit the correlation-vs-age trend and test monotonicity.
main_risk: Archived prediction files may be unavailable or survivorship-biased toward similar high-performing systems, confounding age with selection.
community_default_belief: A one-point gap on a benchmark means the same thing in year one and year five of the benchmark's life.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The population of measured models is itself evolving toward homogeneity, changing both the noise and the meaning of a fixed-size gap.
fastest_falsification: Flat or decreasing error correlation across cohorts on the first two leaderboards examined kills the law.

one_line: Deleting the noisiest tenth of test labels changes absolute scores but leaves model rankings on mature benchmarks essentially intact.
problem: Label-error studies imply benchmarks are compromised, but it is not established whether label noise actually corrupts the comparative conclusions the community draws.
core_hypothesis: Test-label noise on mature benchmarks acts approximately as a rank-preserving offset: pruning or correcting the most disputed items shifts everyone's score but reorders almost no adjacent model pairs beyond resampling noise.
falsifiable_prediction: On benchmarks with published label-error audits, re-scoring public submissions after removing the flagged items will produce rank correlations with the original leaderboard indistinguishable from bootstrap-equivalent rank correlations, except for pairs separated by less than the minimum detectable delta.
why_important: If rankings are noise-robust, expensive relabeling campaigns should be justified by absolute-score needs (e.g., safety thresholds), not by fear of wrong comparative conclusions.
why_possibly_novel: Label-error prevalence is documented; the equivalence claim that comparative conclusions survive noise pruning, stated and tested as a null hypothesis with power analysis, is hypothesized to be rarer (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use an existing label-error audit of one benchmark plus public per-item predictions; re-score with flagged items removed; compare observed rank perturbation against the bootstrap null; pre-register the equivalence margin.
main_risk: The equivalence may hold only where noise is uncorrelated with model differences; benchmarks where errors concentrate in one category could genuinely reorder specialists.
community_default_belief: Widely publicized label-error rates mean benchmark conclusions are unreliable until datasets are cleaned.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Ranking is a paired statistic; noise common to all models cancels in comparisons even when absolute scores are biased.
fastest_falsification: If pruning flagged items reorders many model pairs well above the detectable-delta threshold on the first audited benchmark, the null is dead.

one_line: Bootstrap-over-items confidence intervals systematically understate benchmark uncertainty because they omit the variance of re-collecting the dataset itself.
problem: The field's de facto uncertainty standard (bootstrap over test items) treats the test set as the population, ignoring that the benchmark is one draw from a data-collection process.
core_hypothesis: When a benchmark's collection protocol is replicated end-to-end (new crawl, new annotators, same spec), between-replicate score variance materially exceeds within-replicate bootstrap variance, so published intervals are too narrow by a benchmark-specific factor.
falsifiable_prediction: For at least one small benchmark with a fully documented protocol, three independent re-collections will produce score shifts for the same frozen models exceeding the bootstrap interval width on a majority of models.
why_important: If collection variance dominates, small leaderboard gaps are uninterpretable regardless of test size, and reporting standards should require protocol-replication error bars for benchmark-level claims.
why_possibly_novel: Replication studies exist for a few famous datasets; folding a 'collection variance' term into routine benchmark uncertainty reporting, with a measured within-vs-between decomposition, is hypothesized to be unstandardized (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Choose one cheap-to-collect benchmark (e.g., a small web-image classification task with a written spec); re-collect it three times with disjoint crawlers/annotators; evaluate frozen public models; compare between-replicate variance to mean bootstrap variance.
main_risk: Perfect protocol replication is impossible; critics can attribute between-replicate variance to spec ambiguity rather than genuine sampling variance, though that itself is a benchmark weakness.
community_default_belief: A bootstrap confidence interval over test items is an adequate statement of a benchmark score's uncertainty.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The item bootstrap conditions on one realized dataset and cannot see variance contributed by the collection pipeline, which is part of the measurement instrument.
fastest_falsification: If between-replicate score shifts sit comfortably inside bootstrap intervals for nearly all models, the understatement claim fails.

one_line: Computerized-adaptive-testing item selection can estimate a model's benchmark score to within noise using a small fraction of items, enabling cheap continuous evaluation.
problem: Full-benchmark evaluation of large models is expensive enough that labs evaluate rarely and on few checkpoints, blinding development to regressions between milestones.
core_hypothesis: Because item difficulty and discrimination are stable across models, an adaptive item-selection policy (estimate ability, pick maximally informative next item) reaches the full-benchmark score estimate within its own confidence interval using a small, predictable fraction of items.
falsifiable_prediction: On benchmarks with dense public per-item results, an item-response-theory-driven adaptive tester will match full-set scores within the bootstrap band for held-out models while consuming a minority of the items, beating random subsampling at equal budget.
why_important: Order-of-magnitude cheaper trustworthy evaluation changes evaluation frequency, enabling per-commit benchmark tracking and shrinking the blast radius of silent regressions.
why_possibly_novel: Psychometric adaptive testing is mature; its calibration-transfer failure modes on rapidly shifting model populations, and a working recipe for ML benchmarks, are hypothesized to be underexplored (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fit a 2-parameter IRT model on archived per-item results from one leaderboard; hold out recent submissions; run adaptive testing for the held-out models; compare item budget and error against random subsets.
main_risk: Item parameters drift when a new model family behaves unlike the calibration population, silently corrupting adaptive estimates precisely for the most interesting models.
community_default_belief: Trustworthy benchmark numbers require running the full test set.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Most items carry little marginal information about a given model's ability; the informative subset differs per model and can be found online.
fastest_falsification: If adaptive selection fails to beat random subsampling at equal budget on the first leaderboard, the mechanism adds nothing.

one_line: The number of models a fixed test set can statistically distinguish grows sublinearly with test size, so most leaderboards exceeded their discriminative capacity at a predictable date.
problem: Leaderboards accumulate hundreds of entries, but nobody states how many distinct performance levels a test set of size n can actually resolve.
core_hypothesis: A test set supports only on the order of (score range / minimum detectable delta) distinguishable performance levels, a quantity growing roughly with the square root of n; once entries exceed this capacity, adjacent leaderboard positions are statistically exchangeable.
falsifiable_prediction: Computing per-benchmark capacity from measured item variance and comparing to entry counts will show a crossing date for most long-lived leaderboards, after which the empirical fraction of statistically-tied adjacent pairs rises sharply, matching the capacity model's prediction.
why_important: A capacity number printed on every leaderboard would tell readers which positions are real and give maintainers a principled trigger for refreshing or expanding test sets.
why_possibly_novel: Significance of individual comparisons is discussed, but treating a leaderboard as a channel with finite resolving capacity, with a closed-form capacity estimate validated empirically, is hypothesized to be new framing (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 5 leaderboards with per-item data, compute minimum detectable deltas, derive capacity, and test whether the fraction of exchangeable adjacent pairs over time follows the capacity model rather than growing linearly with entries.
main_risk: Inter-item correlation and heterogeneous submission quality complicate a clean square-root law; capacity may need empirical rather than closed-form calibration.
community_default_belief: More leaderboard entries mean finer-grained community knowledge about method quality.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Information about ordering is bounded by the test set, not by entry count; beyond capacity, new entries add ties, not knowledge.
fastest_falsification: If tied-pair fractions stay flat as entries exceed computed capacity on two leaderboards, the capacity framing is wrong.

one_line: Contamination advantage is mediated by answer memorization, not input familiarity: paraphrasing test inputs while preserving answers removes most of the contaminated model's edge.
problem: Contamination is measured as overlap between training corpora and test sets, but overlap does not identify the mechanism by which contamination inflates scores, so mitigations are unprincipled.
core_hypothesis: The dominant causal path of contamination inflation runs through target memorization (input-answer binding), not through familiarity with input surface forms, so answer-preserving input paraphrase collapses the inflation while input-preserving answer re-derivation does not.
falsifiable_prediction: In a controlled continued-pretraining experiment injecting test items at known rates, evaluating on (a) originals, (b) input-paraphrased, and (c) answer-recomputed variants will show inflation on (a) mostly vanishing under (b) but persisting under (c).
why_important: Identifies which decontamination interventions matter: paraphrase-based eval hardening would be sufficient, whereas expensive corpus-level input matching would be partially misdirected.
why_possibly_novel: Contamination studies typically report score deltas; a factorial dissociation of input-familiarity vs answer-binding channels with controlled injection is hypothesized to be missing (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Continue pretraining a mid-size open model on corpora with injected test items at controlled duplication counts; build paraphrase and answer-recomputation variants of the injected items; measure inflation per variant per duplication count.
main_risk: Paraphrase quality is a confound: bad paraphrases raise difficulty and mimic decontamination; needs human-verified difficulty-matched paraphrases.
community_default_belief: Contamination is fundamentally about the model having 'seen the test data', so matching inputs against corpora is the right detection paradigm.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Seeing inputs without exploitable targets may be nearly harmless; the operative leak is the input-target join, which input-matching detection only proxies.
fastest_falsification: If inflation survives input paraphrase at full strength in the controlled injection study, the memorization-mediation claim is false.

one_line: Because frontier models share the same few web corpora, per-model contamination inflation on public benchmarks is near-uniform, distorting absolute scores but not cross-model comparisons.
problem: Contamination panic treats every leaderboard as invalid, but if all measured models are contaminated to similar degrees, the comparative signal may survive.
core_hypothesis: For models trained on overlapping web-scale corpora, estimated contamination inflation per model is statistically indistinguishable across model families, so decontaminated re-scoring preserves leaderboard orderings within the minimum detectable delta.
falsifiable_prediction: Applying a consistent contamination estimator (e.g., performance gap on n-gram-matched vs unmatched item strata) to many public models will yield per-model inflation estimates whose spread is small relative to between-model score gaps, and decontaminated rankings will match original rankings for pairs above the detectable delta.
why_important: Would redirect contamination effort from relitigating old leaderboards toward protecting future benchmarks, and would restore justified confidence in comparative claims.
why_possibly_novel: Contamination is usually studied per-model or per-benchmark; the cross-model uniformity question, posed as a testable equivalence with explicit margins, is hypothesized to be unexamined (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Stratify 2 benchmarks by corpus-match strength; evaluate ~10 open models spanning families; estimate per-model inflation from stratum gaps; test homogeneity of inflation and rank preservation after correction.
main_risk: Closed-corpus models (proprietary filtering, private data) may break uniformity exactly where public verification is impossible, limiting the claim to open models.
community_default_belief: Contamination invalidates cross-model comparisons on any benchmark that predates the models' training cutoffs.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Comparisons difference away shared inflation; only differential contamination harms rankings, and shared corpora make contamination largely non-differential.
fastest_falsification: If inflation estimates differ severalfold across model families on the first benchmark, contamination is differential and the equivalence dies.

one_line: Benchmarks should ship with watermarked canary items at release; later models' canary behavior yields a per-model contamination score without corpus access.
problem: Contamination detection currently requires access to training corpora, which is unavailable for closed models, leaving the community with no model-side audit instrument.
core_hypothesis: Uniquely constructed no-op canary items (unguessable string-answer bindings with no semantic route to the answer) embedded in a benchmark release produce, in later models, canary recall rates that track those models' score inflation on the benchmark's real items.
falsifiable_prediction: In controlled injection experiments, models trained on corpora containing the benchmark release will exhibit canary recall far above the guessing floor, and across injection doses canary recall will correlate strongly with measured inflation on real items.
why_important: Gives benchmark maintainers a corpus-free, model-side contamination meter, enabling contamination-aware leaderboard annotations for closed models.
why_possibly_novel: Canaries are used for privacy leakage measurement; wiring them into benchmark releases as calibrated contamination dosimeters for evaluation integrity is hypothesized to be unpracticed (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Create a small benchmark with embedded canaries; inject it into continued-pretraining corpora at several doses; measure canary recall vs real-item inflation across doses; verify the dose-response tracks.
main_risk: Deliberate canary filtering by model builders decouples the meter from real contamination; canaries must be indistinguishable from real items to filters.
community_default_belief: Contamination auditing requires inspecting training data, so closed models are unauditable.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The model itself stores the evidence; properly designed probes can read contamination out of behavior without corpus access.
fastest_falsification: If canary recall stays at the guessing floor even under heavy injection, canaries cannot serve as dosimeters.

one_line: Hash-based deduplication misses semantic duplicates (same scene or fact, different rendering), so 'decontaminated' benchmark claims systematically understate leakage.
problem: Decontamination pipelines rely on exact or near-exact matching (n-grams, perceptual hashes), but training-test leakage can flow through semantically equivalent items those methods cannot see.
core_hypothesis: Embedding-based retrieval over training corpora will find, for a material fraction of 'clean' test items, semantic near-duplicates that measurably inflate scores, with the inflation gradient visible across retrieval-similarity strata even within the hash-clean subset.
falsifiable_prediction: On benchmarks previously declared decontaminated by n-gram methods, stratifying hash-clean test items by maximum embedding similarity to training data will show monotonically higher model accuracy in high-similarity strata after controlling for item difficulty proxies.
why_important: If semantic leakage is material, decontamination reports create false confidence, and similarity-stratified scoring should replace binary clean/contaminated labels.
why_possibly_novel: Embedding retrieval for contamination has been explored piecemeal; a quantified comparison showing how much leakage hash-based decontamination certificates miss, expressed as residual score inflation, is hypothesized to be unestablished (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: For one open-corpus model and one 'decontaminated' benchmark, retrieve top-similarity training neighbors per test item with a strong embedding model; bin items by similarity; compare accuracy across bins with difficulty controls (human ratings or IRT difficulty).
main_risk: High similarity correlates with item typicality, which correlates with easiness; difficulty controls must be strong or the gradient is confounded.
community_default_belief: A benchmark that passes n-gram decontamination against a model's corpus provides an uncontaminated measurement of that model.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Models generalize across surface forms, so leakage generalizes too; string matching audits the wrong equivalence class.
fastest_falsification: If accuracy shows no similarity gradient within hash-clean items after difficulty control, the residual-leakage claim collapses.

one_line: Contamination score inflation follows a logarithmic dose-response in duplication count, allowing contamination dose to be estimated from behavior alone.
problem: Contamination is discussed as binary (seen/unseen), but training data contains items at wildly different duplication counts, and the functional form of inflation vs dose is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Score inflation on a contaminated item grows approximately logarithmically with the item's duplication count in the training corpus, with a family-specific slope, so an inverse map from measured inflation to estimated dose exists.
falsifiable_prediction: Controlled injection of benchmark items at duplication counts spanning several orders of magnitude will produce per-item inflation curves well fit by a log law across model scales, with fitted slopes stable enough to invert dose from behavior within a factor of ~3.
why_important: A behavioral dosimeter would let auditors estimate not just whether but how much a benchmark leaked into a closed model, making contamination claims quantitative and adjudicable.
why_possibly_novel: Memorization-vs-duplication curves exist for verbatim text recall; connecting them quantitatively to benchmark score inflation with an invertible dose law is hypothesized to be undone (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Continued-pretraining injections at controlled counts (1, 4, 16, 64, 256) for item batches; fit inflation vs log-count per batch; test out-of-sample dose recovery on held-out injected batches.
main_risk: The law may depend on training schedule position (early vs late exposure) and item type, fragmenting one law into many and weakening inversion.
community_default_belief: Contamination either happened or it did not; a single overlap bit per item is the relevant audit output.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Memorization strength is continuous in exposure; binarizing discards the very signal that would make audits quantitative.
fastest_falsification: If inflation vs log-dose is non-monotonic or wildly item-dependent in the first injection study, no usable law exists.

one_line: Time-split benchmarks overstate generalization because 'future' test items have near-duplicate ancestors in the 'past'; entity-disjoint splits reveal the true gap.
problem: Temporal splits are treated as leakage-proof by construction, but real-world streams (news, products, code) recycle entities and templates across the split boundary.
core_hypothesis: A large fraction of post-cutoff test items are predictable from pre-cutoff near-duplicates (same entity, event series, or template), so time-split scores materially exceed scores on the entity-disjoint subset of the same test period.
falsifiable_prediction: Partitioning time-split test sets into entity-linked vs entity-novel items (via entity linking and template clustering) will show a significant score gap favoring entity-linked items across models, and the headline benchmark score will sit much closer to the entity-linked stratum.
why_important: Temporal evaluation underwrites claims about models handling 'new' information; if those claims mostly measure entity recurrence, downstream reliability estimates for genuinely novel events are inflated.
why_possibly_novel: Temporal leakage is acknowledged qualitatively in some domains; a general entity-disjointness audit quantifying how much of the time-split score is recurrence, across several benchmark genres, is hypothesized to be missing (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take 2 time-split benchmarks; run entity linking between test items and pre-cutoff data; stratify scores by linkage; compare strata gaps and their share of the headline number.
main_risk: Entity linking recall is imperfect; undetected links dilute the measured gap, biasing toward the null.
community_default_belief: Splitting by time guarantees the test measures generalization to unseen data.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Time orders events but does not de-correlate them; the world after the cutoff is substantially a continuation of the world before it.
fastest_falsification: If entity-linked and entity-novel strata score equally on the first benchmark, temporal recurrence is not inflating anything.

one_line: Report benchmark scores per retrieval-similarity-to-training bin: the low-similarity bin is a free decontaminated benchmark requiring no data recollection.
problem: Building fresh decontaminated benchmarks is slow and expensive, while existing benchmarks contain internal variation in training-proximity that scoring conventions throw away.
core_hypothesis: Stratifying any benchmark's items by embedding similarity to a reference training corpus and reporting the low-similarity stratum alongside the headline number yields a contamination-resistant score that better predicts performance on genuinely fresh data.
falsifiable_prediction: Low-similarity-stratum scores will predict model performance on newly collected same-task items (collected after model cutoffs) better than headline scores, with the prediction gap largest for models with the highest estimated contamination.
why_important: Converts every existing benchmark into a partially decontaminated one at the cost of one retrieval pass, giving the community an immediate mitigation while fresh benchmarks are built.
why_possibly_novel: Similarity analyses appear in contamination papers as diagnostics; institutionalizing the low-similarity stratum as a reported score with validated predictive advantages is hypothesized to be unadopted (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 2 benchmarks, compute similarity strata against an open reference corpus; collect a small fresh test set post-cutoff; compare how well headline vs low-similarity scores predict fresh-set performance across ~10 models.
main_risk: Low-similarity items skew hard and atypical, so the stratum measures difficulty shift as well as decontamination; needs difficulty reweighting to isolate the effect.
community_default_belief: Decontaminating evaluation requires building new test sets after each model's training cutoff.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Existing test sets already contain items far from any training data; the information is present and merely unreported.
fastest_falsification: If the low-similarity stratum predicts fresh-data performance no better than the headline score, the stratification buys nothing.

one_line: Realistic leaderboard probing leaks so few bits per submission that measured adaptive-overfitting inflation on large test sets sits below the detection floor.
problem: Theory shows repeated test-set queries can be exploited to overfit holdouts, and the community fears leaderboard probing, but the empirically realized inflation under actual submission behavior is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: Given actual submission counts, score granularity, and test sizes of major leaderboards, the information leaked to any team is small enough that realized probing-induced inflation is statistically undetectable against resampling noise.
falsifiable_prediction: Reconstructing per-team submission histories on leaderboards with logs and comparing public-set gains to private/held-out-set gains will show a public-private generalization gap consistent with zero adaptive overfitting within the noise band for large-test-set leaderboards, with detectable gaps only where test sets are small and submissions dense.
why_important: Would replace diffuse fear of leaderboard gaming with a quantitative boundary (test size x submission budget) inside which current practice is provably safe, informing eval-server design.
why_possibly_novel: Adaptive data analysis theory gives worst-case bounds; an empirical measurement of realized leakage under natural community behavior, framed as an equivalence test with power analysis, is hypothesized to be rare (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Obtain public/private split histories from competition platforms; regress private-public gap on submission count and test size across many competitions; test whether the large-n regime's gap is bounded by the pre-registered equivalence margin.
main_risk: Competition data may not represent research leaderboards, where iteration is offline and unlogged; the equivalence claim is then limited to logged settings.
community_default_belief: Leaderboard probing meaningfully corrupts public benchmark scores, so all public-test numbers are suspect.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Exploiting a holdout requires extracting bits at a rate that realistic submission budgets and score rounding may simply not support.
fastest_falsification: If large-test-set competitions show systematic private-public gaps growing with submission count, probing inflation is real and the null fails.

one_line: The optimal split of a fixed labeling budget between more items and repeated annotation is a computable function of rater disagreement and the model-accuracy regime.
problem: Benchmark builders allocate annotation budget between breadth (more items, single label) and depth (fewer items, multiple raters) by convention, without a decision rule tied to the benchmark's purpose.
core_hypothesis: For ranking models, the variance-minimizing depth-vs-breadth allocation depends only on the rater-noise-to-item-variance ratio and the accuracy regime of the models being compared, yielding a closed-form rule: single-label breadth early (low accuracy), multi-rater depth as models approach the noise ceiling.
falsifiable_prediction: Simulations calibrated on real multi-rater datasets, then a live re-annotation experiment, will show the rule's allocation beating both all-breadth and all-depth baselines in ranking accuracy per label spent, with the crossover point appearing where the rule predicts.
why_important: Annotation is the dominant cost of benchmark construction; a validated allocation law converts folklore into engineering and extends benchmark life exactly when models near the noise ceiling.
why_possibly_novel: Depth-vs-breadth has been studied for training-label collection; a decision rule specific to evaluation (ranking variance, noise-ceiling proximity) validated in a live benchmark setting is hypothesized to be absent (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take a public multi-rater dataset; simulate budget allocations by subsampling raters/items; verify the analytic optimum; then run one modest live collection following the rule vs convention and compare ranking precision on frozen models.
main_risk: Rater noise is item-heterogeneous, not iid; the closed form may need item-difficulty covariates, complicating the rule.
community_default_belief: One label per item, maximizing item count, is the efficient default for benchmark construction.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Once models are near the single-rater noise floor, additional single-labeled items measure noise, and only depth restores discriminative power.
fastest_falsification: If simulated ranking precision is insensitive to allocation across realistic regimes, no rule is needed and the law is vacuous.

one_line: Crowd-majority labels, though noisier than expert labels, are hypothesized to produce the same model rankings as expert relabeling on most natural-image and text tasks.
problem: Crowdsourced benchmarks are routinely dismissed as low-quality relative to expert-labeled ones, but the operational question—do they rank models differently?—is rarely tested head-to-head.
core_hypothesis: Crowd label noise on common perception and language tasks is mostly non-differential with respect to model choice, so expert relabeling shifts absolute scores but reorders model pairs no more than resampling noise, except on expert-knowledge-intensive slices.
falsifiable_prediction: On datasets possessing both crowd and expert label sets (or via targeted expert relabeling of crowd benchmarks), rank correlation of model leaderboards under the two label sources will be statistically indistinguishable from bootstrap-equivalent correlation, with divergence confined to identifiable expert-dependent item strata.
why_important: If crowd labels rank correctly, the community can stop paying expert premiums for comparative evaluation and spend expertise only on the strata that need it, cutting benchmark cost substantially.
why_possibly_novel: Label-quality comparisons usually target accuracy of the labels themselves; the ranking-equivalence question, framed with equivalence margins and stratum localization, is hypothesized to be undertested (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Expert-relabel a random 10-15% of one crowd benchmark plus an oversample of high-disagreement items; re-score public models; test ranking equivalence overall and per stratum.
main_risk: Tasks with genuine expertise gradients (medical, legal) will break the equivalence, and overgeneralizing from natural-image results could mislead those domains.
community_default_belief: Expert-labeled benchmarks are necessary for trustworthy model comparison; crowd benchmarks are second-class evidence.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Ranking is robust to label noise that hits all models symmetrically; the expert premium buys absolute-score accuracy that comparisons do not need.
fastest_falsification: If expert relabeling reorders many model pairs beyond the detectable-delta threshold on a natural-image task, the rehabilitation fails there.

one_line: Relabeling only the items where top models disagree with each other repairs benchmark headroom estimates at a small fraction of full-relabel cost.
problem: Full benchmark relabeling campaigns are so expensive they rarely happen, leaving stale label errors to distort headroom and near-tie comparisons indefinitely.
core_hypothesis: Label errors that matter for current-model comparison and headroom estimation concentrate where strong models disagree with each other or with labels, so an audit budget targeted by model-committee disagreement recovers most ranking corrections and headroom corrections at a small budget fraction.
falsifiable_prediction: On a benchmark with an existing full label audit, replaying targeted selection (disagreement-ranked) will recover the large majority of audit-induced score corrections and rank changes while auditing a small minority of items, beating random auditing at equal budget by a wide margin.
why_important: Makes benchmark maintenance an affordable recurring operation instead of a heroic one-off, directly extending the trustworthy life of widely used evaluations.
why_possibly_novel: Model-assisted label-error detection exists; validating a maintenance policy against a full-audit ground truth, with recovery curves and budget rules for maintainers, is hypothesized to be unquantified (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use one benchmark with a published full audit; simulate disagreement-targeted vs random relabel budgets; compute recovery curves for score and rank corrections; report the budget at 90% recovery.
main_risk: Consensus errors (all models wrong the same way) are invisible to disagreement targeting and remain unrepaired, understating residual error.
community_default_belief: Cleaning a benchmark requires re-examining substantially all of it, which is why it is rarely done.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The errors that affect current conclusions are localized by current models' behavior; the rest are dormant with respect to today's comparisons.
fastest_falsification: If disagreement-targeted auditing recovers corrections at no better than the random-audit rate, targeting is useless.

one_line: A benchmark's label error rate imposes a computable score ceiling, and the distance between top models and that ceiling forecasts how much remaining 'headroom' is real.
problem: Communities chase the gap between the best model and a perfect score without knowing what portion of that gap is achievable given label errors in the test set.
core_hypothesis: Given an estimated label-error rate and error structure, the maximum measurable score is a computable ceiling; across benchmarks, progress decelerates sharply as leaders approach this ceiling, and the ceiling-adjusted headroom predicts future score gains better than raw headroom.
falsifiable_prediction: Estimating ceilings for many benchmarks via label-audit samples, then regressing subsequent-period leaderboard gains on ceiling-adjusted vs raw headroom, will show the adjusted quantity is the substantially better predictor.
why_important: Turns 'is this benchmark done?' into a calculation, informing when a community should re-invest in labels versus retire the benchmark versus keep pushing models.
why_possibly_novel: Label-noise ceilings are computed occasionally for single datasets; a cross-benchmark predictive validation that adjusted headroom forecasts realized progress is hypothesized to be new (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Audit ~200 items on each of 6 benchmarks at different maturity; compute ceilings; use historical leaderboard data to test whether adjusted headroom predicts next-period gains out-of-sample.
main_risk: Ceilings depend on error structure (random vs systematic), and a small audit may misestimate structure, propagating into bad ceilings.
community_default_belief: The gap to a perfect score represents room for modeling progress.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Part of that gap is unreachable measurement error; treating it as headroom misallocates research effort toward chasing noise.
fastest_falsification: If adjusted and raw headroom predict future gains equally well, the ceiling adds no information.

one_line: Gold-question quality control selects raters for conformity with the gold authors, homogenizing the pool and imprinting the authors' biases on ambiguous items.
problem: Gold-question filtering is the industry-standard annotation QC mechanism, assumed to remove bad raters while leaving the label distribution otherwise unbiased.
core_hypothesis: Because gold questions are authored by a small team, passing them selects raters whose priors match the authors', so gold-filtered pools show reduced inter-rater diversity on ambiguous items and shift ambiguous-item majority labels toward the gold authors' own answers relative to unfiltered pools.
falsifiable_prediction: Running parallel annotation of the same item set with gold-filtered and attention-check-only pools will show (a) lower entropy of label distributions on high-ambiguity items in the gold-filtered pool and (b) a measurable shift of majority labels toward gold-author answers on a held-out set the authors also labeled.
why_important: If QC injects authorial bias, benchmarks inherit a hidden single-team prior at scale, and downstream 'human agreement' statistics overstate consensus.
why_possibly_novel: Rater-quality filtering is studied for accuracy effects; its selection effect on the opinion distribution over ambiguous items, treated as a benchmark-bias mechanism, is hypothesized to be unmeasured (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Recruit one large rater pool; randomly assign gold-filter vs attention-check-only QC; annotate a shared set including high-ambiguity items and gold-author-labeled holdouts; compare label entropy and author-alignment across arms.
main_risk: Attention-check-only pools include genuinely careless raters whose noise could mimic 'diversity', requiring careful separation of care from opinion.
community_default_belief: Gold-question filtering removes noise without changing what the honest labels would have been.
why_that_may_be_wrong: On items where honest humans disagree, any filter keyed to 'correct' answers is a filter on opinions, not just on effort.
fastest_falsification: If gold-filtered and attention-only pools produce identical label distributions on ambiguous items, the selection-bias mechanism is absent.

one_line: Beyond a minimal core, longer annotation guidelines do not reduce inter-rater disagreement on ambiguous items; disagreement is intrinsic to items, not instructions.
problem: Benchmark builders respond to disagreement by lengthening guidelines, assuming disagreement reflects under-specification that more rules can remove.
core_hypothesis: Inter-rater disagreement decomposes into an instruction-reducible component that saturates with a short guideline and an intrinsic-ambiguity component that no guideline length removes; on typical perception and judgment tasks the intrinsic component dominates for the contested items.
falsifiable_prediction: A randomized trial assigning raters to guideline versions of increasing length will show disagreement on pre-identified contested items flat (within equivalence margin) beyond the short-core version, while total annotation time grows with guideline length.
why_important: Would redirect QC investment from rule-writing to distribution-aware labeling (collecting and shipping the disagreement) and would reinterpret disagreement metrics as item properties rather than process failures.
why_possibly_novel: Guideline effects are usually evaluated anecdotally during dataset construction; a controlled guideline-length dose-response with equivalence testing on contested strata is hypothesized to be unrun (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Write four guideline versions (core, +examples, +edge-case rules, +full decision tree) for one task; randomize raters; measure per-stratum disagreement and time; test equivalence beyond the core version.
main_risk: Guideline effects may interact with rater training and tenure; short-exposure trials could understate the value long guidelines have for career annotators.
community_default_belief: Disagreement in annotation signals that the guidelines need more rules and examples.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Where the world itself is ambiguous, additional rules relocate disagreement to rule-interpretation instead of removing it.
fastest_falsification: If disagreement on contested items drops materially with each guideline extension, the intrinsic-dominance claim is wrong.

one_line: Ship per-item rater distributions as 'ambiguity certificates' and score models against distributions; distribution-scored rankings will diverge from majority-label rankings exactly on high-ambiguity slices.
problem: Benchmarks compress multi-rater judgments into single majority labels, destroying the ambiguity information and forcing models to be graded against manufactured certainty.
core_hypothesis: Publishing per-item label distributions and scoring models by distributional agreement (proper scoring rules against the rater distribution) yields a different and more deployment-relevant ordering on ambiguous strata, while agreeing with majority-label scoring on unambiguous strata.
falsifiable_prediction: On existing multi-rater datasets, distribution-scored and majority-scored rankings will agree closely on low-entropy items and diverge beyond resampling noise on high-entropy items, and the distribution-scored ranking will better predict human preference in a downstream task where ambiguity matters (e.g., content moderation triage).
why_important: Gives benchmarks a principled way to stop punishing models for honest probability mass on genuinely contested items, and creates incentives for calibrated rather than mode-seeking predictions.
why_possibly_novel: Learning-from-disagreement literature exists; the benchmark-engineering package (certificates as release artifacts, dual scoring, divergence localization, downstream validation) is hypothesized to be unassembled (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-score public models on 2 multi-rater datasets under both schemes; quantify ranking divergence by entropy stratum; run one small downstream human study testing which ranking predicts perceived model quality on ambiguous content.
main_risk: Rater distributions confound ambiguity with pool composition; certificates may need pool metadata to be interpretable across benchmarks.
community_default_belief: A benchmark must provide one correct label per item; disagreement is upstream noise to be resolved before release.
why_that_may_be_wrong: For contested items the distribution is the ground truth; collapsing it discards the target that deployment actually cares about.
fastest_falsification: If dual scoring never diverges beyond noise even on high-entropy strata, the certificates change nothing.

one_line: Rater error rates follow a reproducible within-session fatigue curve, so item position in annotation logs predicts label reliability item by item.
problem: Benchmarks treat all labels from an accepted rater as equally reliable, ignoring that annotation happens in long sessions with known human vigilance dynamics.
core_hypothesis: Label error probability rises with within-session position following a stable two-phase curve (warm-up then fatigue), consistent across raters up to a scale factor, so session logs enable per-label reliability weights without any re-annotation.
falsifiable_prediction: On datasets with session logs and partial gold overlap, fitting error rate vs session position will reveal the two-phase shape with significant fatigue slopes; reweighting labels by fitted reliability will improve agreement with held-out expert labels compared to uniform weighting.
why_important: A free reliability covariate hiding in existing logs would let maintainers upgrade label quality retroactively and design session lengths that cap error rates by policy.
why_possibly_novel: Vigilance decrement is established in human-factors research; importing it as a quantitative, log-derived per-label reliability model for benchmark construction is hypothesized to be unexploited (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Obtain session-ordered logs with embedded gold items from one large annotation effort; fit position-error curves per rater cohort; validate reweighting on expert-relabeled holdout.
main_risk: Item difficulty may correlate with position (queues often batch similar items), confounding fatigue with content; needs difficulty controls or randomized queues.
community_default_belief: Once a rater passes quality control, their labels are homogeneous in quality.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Human error is a within-session process, not a fixed trait; QC measures the rater's average, not the trajectory.
fastest_falsification: If position-error curves are flat on randomized-queue data, fatigue structure is negligible and the weighting is pointless.

one_line: A decade of feared test-set reuse produced far less adaptive overfitting than theory permits: fresh replicate test sets will reproduce original rankings nearly unchanged.
problem: The community assumes years of hill-climbing on famous fixed test sets has corrupted them, but the realized (as opposed to worst-case) overfitting on major benchmarks is largely unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: Community-scale test-set reuse acts mostly through slow architecture/recipe evolution rather than per-item exploitation, so replicate test sets collected to original protocols preserve model rankings, with absolute score drops explained by distribution shift rather than overfitting-to-items.
falsifiable_prediction: For several benchmarks where replicate collection is feasible, rank correlation between original and replicate leaderboards will be near the bootstrap ceiling, and the score drop will be uncorrelated with the number of years a model's lineage hill-climbed on the benchmark.
why_important: If reuse is benign at community scale, aggressive test-set secrecy and rotation policies are solving a smaller problem than assumed, and old benchmarks' comparative conclusions deserve rehabilitation.
why_possibly_novel: Replication studies exist for select benchmarks; generalizing to a law ('reuse inflation is second-order across genres') with a lineage-exposure regression as the falsification lever is hypothesized to be untested (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-collect small replicate test sets for 2 benchmarks in different genres; evaluate a lineage-annotated model set; test rank preservation and the exposure-inflation regression.
main_risk: Genres differ: leaderboards with tiny test sets and dense submission feedback may show real exploitation, making the law genre-conditional.
community_default_belief: Long-lived public test sets are badly overfit, and scores on them no longer reflect real capability differences.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Per-item information leaks slowly through publication-mediated feedback, and model development optimizes recipes against distributions, not memorized items.
fastest_falsification: If replicate rankings scramble or score drops track lineage exposure, community-scale overfitting is real and the rehabilitation dies.

one_line: Benchmark lifetime is predictable at release: time-to-saturation scales with the initial human-model gap and the community submission rate in a fittable law.
problem: Benchmarks die unpredictably, and the community learns of saturation only after wasting cycles on a spent instrument; no quantitative model of benchmark lifespan exists.
core_hypothesis: Across historical benchmarks, time-to-saturation (leader within noise of the ceiling) follows a scaling relation in two release-time observables—initial gap between best baseline and estimated ceiling, and early submission velocity—accurate enough to forecast lifespan within a factor of two.
falsifiable_prediction: Fitting the relation on a retrospective corpus of finished benchmarks will predict held-out benchmarks' saturation dates within the stated tolerance, and will outperform naive baselines (mean lifespan, gap-only, velocity-only).
why_important: Lifespan forecasts would let maintainers schedule refreshes and successor collection before saturation, and let funders time benchmark investments rationally.
why_possibly_novel: Saturation is discussed post hoc; a predictive lifespan law validated out-of-sample across genres is hypothesized to be unbuilt (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble saturation dates, initial gaps, and submission-rate histories for ~30 finished benchmarks from public leaderboard archives; fit and cross-validate the law; pre-register predictions for currently active benchmarks.
main_risk: Regime changes (foundation-model jumps) create lifespan discontinuities no smooth law captures; the law may hold only within technology eras.
community_default_belief: How long a benchmark stays useful is essentially unpredictable, driven by unforeseeable modeling breakthroughs.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Aggregate community progress on a fixed target may behave like a driven relaxation process whose rate constants are visible at release time.
fastest_falsification: If cross-validated predictions do no better than the mean-lifespan baseline, there is no law.

one_line: Late-stage benchmark progress concentrates on label-disputed items: gains after the 90%-of-ceiling point come disproportionately from matching idiosyncratic labels experts contest.
problem: Score gains near saturation are reported as continued progress, but which items supply those gains, and whether their labels are sound, is rarely examined.
core_hypothesis: Decomposing leaderboard progress item-wise will show early-era gains spread across uncontested items while late-era gains concentrate on items with high expert dispute rates, implying late 'progress' substantially measures adaptation to annotation idiosyncrasy.
falsifiable_prediction: For benchmarks with archived per-item predictions across eras and a fresh expert-dispute audit, the dispute rate of 'newly solved' items will rise significantly across eras, and removing disputed items will flatten late-era progress much more than early-era progress.
why_important: If true, saturation should be declared earlier than raw curves suggest, and late-era leaderboard wins should be discounted in method-adoption decisions.
why_possibly_novel: Label errors and saturation are separately documented; the temporal claim that progress migrates toward disputed items as benchmarks age is hypothesized to be untested (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pick one long-lived benchmark with archived submissions; identify items solved in each era; expert-audit a stratified sample of each era's newly-solved items for dispute rate; compare across eras.
main_risk: Newly solved late-era items are also intrinsically harder; hardness and disputedness must be disentangled by the audit design.
community_default_belief: A rising leaderboard curve means models keep getting better at the underlying task.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Near the noise ceiling, the remaining unsolved items are enriched for label problems, so the curve's tail measures agreement with noise.
fastest_falsification: If dispute rates of newly solved items are constant across eras, the migration claim is false.

one_line: Anchor-item designs let living benchmarks refresh content while keeping decade-scale progress curves comparable through psychometric score equating.
problem: When benchmarks refresh their test sets, historical comparability breaks, so the community faces a false choice between stale-but-comparable and fresh-but-incommensurable evaluations.
core_hypothesis: Retaining a calibrated overlap of anchor items across versions and applying standard test-equating transforms preserves cross-version score comparability within quantifiable error, enabling indefinitely refreshable benchmarks with continuous progress curves.
falsifiable_prediction: In a designed experiment creating two overlapping versions of one benchmark, equated scores of frozen models evaluated on both versions will agree within the equating method's stated error bars, while unequated scores will disagree materially.
why_important: Removes the main structural reason benchmarks are left to rot (fear of breaking comparability), enabling routine refresh as standard maintenance.
why_possibly_novel: Equating is routine in educational testing; a worked, validated port to ML benchmark versioning—including anchor sizing rules under model-population shift—is hypothesized to be missing (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Split one large benchmark into two overlapping 'versions' with a controlled anchor set; evaluate ~15 models on both; compare equated vs raw cross-version agreement as a function of anchor size.
main_risk: Equating assumes anchor items measure the same construct for new model populations; contamination of anchors over time erodes exactly the items comparability depends on.
community_default_belief: Refreshing a test set necessarily resets the clock on historical comparisons.
why_that_may_be_wrong: A century of psychometrics exists precisely because comparability across changing test forms is achievable with designed overlap.
fastest_falsification: If equated cross-version scores disagree beyond stated error even with generous anchors, the port fails.

one_line: Successor benchmarks rarely change the ordering: method rankings on a retired benchmark strongly predict rankings on its harder successor.
problem: Communities invest heavily in successor benchmarks assuming harder tests will reveal different winners, but whether succession actually reorders methods is an open empirical question.
core_hypothesis: Within a task family, the latent ability measured by a benchmark and its successor is nearly one-dimensional, so pre-succession rankings predict post-succession rankings up to noise, and succession mainly restores score dynamic range rather than discovering new orderings.
falsifiable_prediction: Across historical benchmark-successor pairs, the rank correlation of methods evaluated on both will be high and statistically indistinguishable from the within-benchmark bootstrap ceiling for the majority of pairs, with exceptions concentrated where the successor changed task format rather than difficulty.
why_important: If succession preserves order, cheaper interventions (rescaling, item refresh) achieve most of a successor's value, and 'new benchmark reveals new winners' narratives need re-examination.
why_possibly_novel: Individual anecdotes exist both ways; a systematic census of succession events with equivalence testing and a format-change moderator analysis is hypothesized to be undone (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Identify ~15 benchmark-successor pairs across CV and NLP with overlapping evaluated methods; compute cross-benchmark rank correlations; pre-register the equivalence margin and the format-change moderator hypothesis.
main_risk: Methods evaluated on both benchmarks are a survivor-biased sample; correcting for selection may require re-running older methods on successors.
community_default_belief: Harder successor benchmarks separate methods that the saturated predecessor could no longer distinguish, changing who wins.
why_that_may_be_wrong: If ability is one-dimensional within the family, difficulty changes the spacing of scores, not the order of methods.
fastest_falsification: If a majority of succession events show rank correlation well below the bootstrap ceiling absent format changes, succession genuinely reorders and the null dies.

one_line: The variance of year-over-year SOTA improvements shrinks along a predictable envelope as benchmarks saturate, enabling statistical detection of the saturation phase-change.
problem: Saturation is declared informally and late; the community lacks a statistical early-warning signal computable from public leaderboard histories alone.
core_hypothesis: SOTA increment sequences behave like a decaying extreme-value process: increment variance contracts along a lawful envelope as the ceiling approaches, and a changepoint in the envelope's decay rate marks entry into the saturation regime well before the curve visibly flattens.
falsifiable_prediction: Fitting the envelope model to historical leaderboards will detect changepoints that precede conventionally recognized saturation dates for most benchmarks, and out-of-sample application to active leaderboards will forecast which saturate next better than curve-flatness heuristics.
why_important: An early quantitative saturation alarm lets communities commission successor benchmarks before the old one distorts research incentives in its degenerate endgame.
why_possibly_novel: Leaderboard curves are plotted constantly; modeling the increment process with extreme-value statistics for changepoint detection is hypothesized to be unattempted (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble SOTA time series for ~40 leaderboards; fit the increment-envelope model; validate changepoint lead-time against expert-annotated saturation dates; run a forward test on active leaderboards.
main_risk: Discontinuous capability jumps (new pretraining paradigms) violate the smooth-envelope assumption, causing false 'unsaturation' resets.
community_default_belief: Saturation can only be recognized in hindsight once the curve has been flat for a while.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The statistical structure of increments carries forward-looking information the raw curve level does not.
fastest_falsification: If detected changepoints show no systematic lead over visible flattening across the corpus, the alarm has no value.

one_line: Methods developed on 'gameable' static benchmarks nonetheless transfer their ordering to freshly collected same-domain data: gaming inflated scores, not ranks.
problem: A prevalent narrative holds that benchmark gaming has corrupted the field's method comparisons, implying years of conclusions are unsound, but the rank-level damage is rarely quantified.
core_hypothesis: Benchmark-era method innovations retain their relative ordering when re-evaluated on newly collected data drawn from the same domain specification, indicating that whatever gaming occurred acted mostly as a shared score offset rather than differential rank corruption.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-evaluating a chronologically diverse set of published methods on freshly collected same-spec data will yield rank correlation with original leaderboard order near the noise ceiling, and any exceptions will be traceable to identifiable benchmark-specific tricks (e.g., exploiting known artifacts) rather than broad decay.
why_important: Rehabilitates the evidentiary status of a decade of comparative results and localizes genuine gaming to enumerable techniques that audits can flag, rather than indicting everything.
why_possibly_novel: Fresh-data replications exist for a few benchmarks with a focus on absolute score drops; the rank-preservation reading as a systematic rehabilitation claim, with trick-attribution for exceptions, is hypothesized to be unargued (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select one benchmark family with reproducible public methods spanning eras; collect a modest fresh same-spec test set; re-evaluate all methods; compute rank preservation and audit outlier methods for artifact exploitation.
main_risk: Reproducing older methods faithfully is hard; implementation drift could masquerade as rank instability.
community_default_belief: Static benchmarks got gamed, so the method rankings they produced are untrustworthy.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Most 'gaming' techniques (tuning, augmentation, ensembling) raise scores for reasons that partially generalize; rank corruption requires differential exploitation, which may be rare.
fastest_falsification: If fresh-data re-evaluation scrambles rankings broadly rather than at identifiable outliers, the rehabilitation fails.

one_line: Maintainers should inject re-rendered 'trap' twins of existing test items each cycle; the trap-original score gap over time is a longitudinal overfitting monitor.
problem: There is no running instrument that tells a benchmark maintainer how much community overfitting to specific test items has accumulated; audits are one-off heroics.
core_hypothesis: Periodically adding semantically equivalent but surface-renewed twins of randomly chosen existing items (re-photographed, re-worded, re-rendered) creates a paired probe: the average original-minus-twin score gap across submissions estimates item-specific overfitting, and its time series tracks accumulation.
falsifiable_prediction: On a leaderboard where twins are silently introduced, the original-twin gap will be near zero for models predating the originals' release and will grow with model release date for items long in circulation, if and only if item-level overfitting is occurring; a flat gap across cohorts certifies its absence.
why_important: Converts the perennial 'is our benchmark still valid?' debate into a dashboard metric with known statistical properties, cheaply maintained as part of normal refresh cycles.
why_possibly_novel: Paraphrase-based robustness probes exist as one-off studies; institutionalizing paired twins as a longitudinal maintenance instrument with cohort analysis is hypothesized to be unimplemented (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Create twins for a random 5% of one benchmark; evaluate a release-date-spanning model set; verify the gap-vs-cohort analysis distinguishes a deliberately overfit model (fine-tuned on test items) from clean models.
main_risk: Twin construction changes difficulty subtly; the design needs human difficulty-matching validation or the gap conflates rendering artifacts with overfitting.
community_default_belief: Detecting test-set overfitting requires collecting an entirely new test set and comparing scores.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Paired surface-renewal isolates item-specific memorization at far lower cost than full re-collection, because each twin controls for its own content.
fastest_falsification: If a deliberately test-set-fine-tuned model shows no original-twin gap, the instrument cannot detect even gross overfitting.

one_line: A small sliver of test items carries most of the rank information on major benchmarks, so unexamined composition choices on that sliver silently decide leaderboards.
problem: Benchmark composition is audited for category balance and size, but not for where the model-discriminating information actually lives within the test set.
core_hypothesis: Per-item discrimination is heavy-tailed: a minority of items accounts for the majority of variance in model rankings, and these items are not the ones composition policies attend to, making leaderboard outcomes hostage to incidental curation decisions.
falsifiable_prediction: Computing item-level discrimination from public per-item results will show that removing a small top-discrimination fraction collapses many adjacent rank distinctions, while removing an equal random fraction leaves rankings intact; the high-discrimination sliver will be demographically and topically unrepresentative of the full set.
why_important: If rankings hinge on an unexamined sliver, benchmark governance should audit and deliberately design that sliver, and readers should know which items their conclusions rest on.
why_possibly_novel: Item discrimination is standard psychometrics; the composition-governance implication—that curation policy ignores exactly the items that decide outcomes—is hypothesized to be undocumented for ML benchmarks (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 3 benchmarks with per-item public results, estimate discrimination per item; run ablations removing top-discrimination vs random slices; characterize the high-discrimination items' provenance and content.
main_risk: Discrimination estimates depend on the model population; the sliver may shift as models evolve, complicating governance.
community_default_belief: With thousands of test items, no small subset materially controls who wins.
why_that_may_be_wrong: When strong models agree on most items, ranking variance is generated only where they disagree, which can be a very small, arbitrary set.
fastest_falsification: If removing the top-discrimination sliver perturbs rankings no more than random removal, the concentration claim is false.

one_line: Class-frequency tails in curated datasets follow the collection interface, not the world: search-collected corpora have systematically flatter tails than passively captured ones by a stable factor.
problem: Long-tail claims about the visual and textual world are routinely made from datasets whose tail shape may be an artifact of how items were gathered.
core_hypothesis: Collection interfaces impose characteristic frequency-spectrum transforms: query-driven collection flattens tails (each query yields a quota regardless of world frequency) while passive capture preserves them, and the transform between the two regimes is stable enough to estimate and invert.
falsifiable_prediction: Comparing category frequency spectra for matched taxonomies across search-collected and passively captured datasets will show a systematic spectrum ratio well fit by a single interface-dependent transform, reproducible across domains, enabling correction of tail statistics for collection mode.
why_important: Long-tail benchmarks calibrate robustness research; if their tails are interface artifacts, both the difficulty claims and the transfer expectations built on them need correction factors.
why_possibly_novel: Dataset bias is a classic topic; a quantitative, invertible interface-transform law for frequency spectra, validated across domains, is hypothesized to be unformulated (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble matched-category frequency data from one search-collected and one passive-capture dataset in each of two domains (driving scenes, household objects); fit the spectrum transform; test cross-domain reproducibility.
main_risk: Taxonomy matching across datasets is lossy, and passive-capture datasets have their own deployment biases, muddying the 'world reference'.
community_default_belief: Large curated datasets approximate the world's category frequency distribution well enough for tail research.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Curation pipelines are frequency filters; what looks like the world's tail is the pipeline's transfer function applied to it.
fastest_falsification: If spectrum ratios between collection modes are unsystematic across domains, no correctable law exists.

one_line: Release test sets with calibrated difficulty strata (from rater disagreement or response time) so cross-benchmark comparisons can use score equating like standardized testing.
problem: Scores on different benchmarks are incomparable because difficulty composition is uncontrolled and undocumented, yet the community constantly compares across them informally.
core_hypothesis: Publishing per-item difficulty calibration (anchored in human measurements such as rater disagreement and response time) at release enables difficulty-equated cross-benchmark score translation whose accuracy can be validated on models evaluated on multiple benchmarks.
falsifiable_prediction: Difficulty-equated score translations between benchmark pairs will predict a model's score on benchmark B from its score on benchmark A substantially better than naive score mapping, with the residual shrinking as strata calibration quality improves.
why_important: Would let the field aggregate evidence across benchmarks in a principled way, weakening single-benchmark monopolies and their idiosyncratic biases.
why_possibly_novel: Difficulty estimation appears in isolated papers; difficulty calibration as a release-artifact standard with validated cross-benchmark equating is hypothesized to be unestablished (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Calibrate difficulty strata for two same-task benchmarks using shared human measurement protocols; fit equating on half the model population; test prediction error on the other half against naive mapping.
main_risk: Human difficulty and model difficulty diverge (see item-response findings elsewhere); equating anchored to human measures may fail exactly for frontier models.
community_default_belief: Cross-benchmark score comparisons are inherently informal; each benchmark is its own incommensurable scale.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Incommensurability is an artifact of missing calibration data, not a property of the tasks; testing science solved this problem where stakes demanded it.
fastest_falsification: If equated translation beats naive mapping by nothing on the first benchmark pair, the calibration artifacts are not worth shipping.

one_line: Geographic and source skew in web-collected benchmarks distorts absolute scores but is hypothesized to leave object-centric model rankings stable across regional slices.
problem: Source-skew critiques are read as invalidating comparative conclusions from web-collected benchmarks, but slice-wise rank stability—the operative question for method choice—is seldom tested.
core_hypothesis: For object-centric recognition tasks, model rankings computed within geographic or source slices agree with the global ranking up to sampling noise, because architectural and training advances are hypothesized to help roughly uniformly across regions; skew therefore biases claimed accuracy levels, not method comparisons.
falsifiable_prediction: Slicing web-collected benchmarks by inferred region/source and re-ranking public models per slice will show cross-slice rank correlations at the bootstrap ceiling for object-centric tasks, with violations concentrated in tasks with region-specific semantics (text in images, cultural artifacts).
why_important: Separates two critiques with different remedies: absolute-score bias (needs representative data or reweighting) versus comparative corruption (would need slice-stratified leaderboards); resources should go where the real problem is.
why_possibly_novel: Geographic bias studies document accuracy gaps across regions; the rank-stability question across slices, with a semantics-dependence moderator, is hypothesized to be unexamined (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Annotate region/source for samples of 2 web benchmarks; evaluate ~15 models per slice; test cross-slice rank agreement with equivalence margins; contrast object-centric vs semantics-heavy tasks.
main_risk: Slice sample sizes limit power; rank equivalence within noisy small slices may be unfalsifiable without targeted data expansion.
community_default_belief: Geographically skewed benchmarks produce conclusions that do not hold for underrepresented regions, including which model is better.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Accuracy gaps across regions can coexist with perfectly preserved orderings if all models share the skew's effects roughly equally.
fastest_falsification: If per-slice rankings on an object-centric task diverge beyond noise, the rehabilitation is wrong for exactly the claimed domain.
