one_line: Class-balanced versus natural-frequency test weighting changes model rankings only when compared models differ in long-tail-specific machinery, an identifiable and rare condition.
problem: Communities argue about whether test sets should be class-balanced or naturally distributed, assuming the choice materially affects who wins.
core_hypothesis: For most model pairs, per-class accuracy profiles are similar enough that reweighting between balanced and natural test distributions preserves pairwise orderings; divergence requires the pair to differ specifically in tail-class mechanisms, which can be detected in advance from per-class profiles.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-scoring public leaderboards under both weightings will show pairwise rank flips confined to model pairs whose per-class accuracy profiles diverge in the tail beyond a computable threshold, with the majority of pairs order-stable under both weightings.
why_important: Would defuse a recurring benchmark-design controversy by showing the choice matters only in predictable cases, and would give a pre-test for when to report both weightings.
why_possibly_novel: Effects of class imbalance on absolute metrics are well studied; a conditional equivalence theorem-plus-census at the ranking level, with a divergence pre-test, is hypothesized to be missing (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 3 classification benchmarks with per-class results available, re-score under both weightings; identify rank-flipped pairs; test whether the tail-divergence statistic separates flipped from stable pairs.
main_risk: The claim's usefulness depends on tail-divergent pairs being rare; if long-tail methods proliferate, the equivalence covers a shrinking share of comparisons.
community_default_belief: The balanced-vs-natural test distribution decision is fundamental to benchmark validity and shapes leaderboard outcomes.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Reweighting is a linear operation on per-class accuracies; orderings survive unless profiles cross, and profile crossings are concentrated in the tail machinery few model pairs differ on.
fastest_falsification: If rank flips under reweighting are common among pairs with similar tail profiles, the pre-test fails and the equivalence is empty.

one_line: Benchmarks built with model-in-the-loop hard-negative mining encode the collector model's blind spots, systematically favoring architectures dissimilar to the collector.
problem: Model-assisted curation (mining hard negatives, filtering easy items) is now standard for making benchmarks challenging, but its effect on the fairness of the resulting comparisons is unexamined.
core_hypothesis: Items selected because a collector model failed them over-represent that model family's characteristic errors, so the benchmark measures dissimilarity-to-collector in addition to capability, granting a structural advantage to architecturally distant models.
falsifiable_prediction: On benchmarks documenting their collector model, evaluated models' scores will correlate negatively with representational similarity to the collector (measured by prediction agreement on neutral data), after controlling for capability on independently collected tasks; re-mining the same source pool with a different collector will produce a benchmark whose ranking shifts in the predicted direction.
why_important: Adversarially mined benchmarks steer method development; if they encode collector-relative rather than absolute difficulty, the field may be optimizing to be unlike one particular model lineage.
why_possibly_novel: Adversarial collection is known to target the loop model; the generalization that residual bias systematically distorts third-party rankings, with a similarity-controlled test and re-mining intervention, is hypothesized to be undemonstrated (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take a source pool and mine two benchmark variants with two different collector families; evaluate a common model set on both; test whether ranking differences align with collector-similarity as predicted.
main_risk: Representational similarity and capability are correlated in the wild; disentangling requires careful capability controls or the effect is unidentifiable.
community_default_belief: Hard-negative mining just concentrates difficulty; the resulting benchmark is a harder but neutral test.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Difficulty defined by one model's failures is a fingerprint of that model; neutrality would require failure consensus across diverse models.
fastest_falsification: If two differently-collected variants rank the common model set identically, collector imprint is negligible.

one_line: The marginal ranking-information value of a test item depends on its source novelty: items from an unrepresented source are worth many items from saturated sources, by a fittable exchange rate.
problem: Test sets grow by accretion from convenient sources, with no quantitative account of how much evaluative information each added item actually contributes.
core_hypothesis: Because items within a source share latent factors, ranking information grows sublinearly in items-per-source but nearly linearly in sources; the items-to-sources exchange rate is estimable from inter-item correlation and stable enough to guide collection budgets.
falsifiable_prediction: Subsampling experiments on multi-source benchmarks will show ranking precision as a function of (items, sources) matching the correlated-information model, with adding a new source improving rank precision as much as a predicted multiple of within-source items.
why_important: Gives benchmark builders a defensible answer to 'collect more from where we already are, or pay the overhead of a new source?', currently decided by convenience.
why_possibly_novel: Cluster-correlated sampling theory is classical; its application as a benchmark design law with validated exchange rates for ML evaluation is hypothesized to be absent (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: On 2 benchmarks with source metadata, subsample grids over items-per-source and source counts; measure ranking precision against the full-set ranking; fit and cross-validate the exchange-rate model.
main_risk: Source boundaries are fuzzy (one website, many photographers); poorly defined clusters could make the fitted rate meaningless.
community_default_belief: Test-set informativeness is measured by item count; ten thousand items is ten times better than one thousand.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Correlated items are partial replays of each other; effective sample size follows cluster structure, not raw count.
fastest_falsification: If ranking precision follows raw item count regardless of source structure, the exchange rate is unity and the law trivializes.

one_line: Benchmark cards should publish per-slice minimum detectable effects; most published slice-level fairness claims are hypothesized to be underpowered by their own benchmark's arithmetic.
problem: Slice-level claims (fairness gaps, robustness by subgroup) are made on subsamples far smaller than the full test set, without any power statement, and readers cannot tell findings from noise.
core_hypothesis: Computing and publishing the minimum detectable effect per slice at release (a 'power column' in the benchmark card) would show that a large share of slice-level comparisons the literature makes on that benchmark are underpowered, and its adoption would measurably change which claims get published.
falsifiable_prediction: A retrospective audit computing per-slice minimum detectable effects for popular benchmarks, then re-examining published slice claims against them, will find a substantial fraction of claims below their own benchmark's detection floor; those claims will replicate at chance rates in re-tests on enlarged slices.
why_important: Slice claims drive policy-relevant conclusions about model bias; a power-audit infrastructure would prevent a class of irreproducible findings at the source.
why_possibly_novel: Power analysis is standard statistics; systematically attaching it to benchmark releases and auditing the literature's slice claims against it is hypothesized to be undone (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute per-slice detection floors for 3 benchmarks; sample ~30 published slice-level claims using them; classify claims by power adequacy; re-test a subsample of underpowered claims with expanded slice data.
main_risk: Effect-size conventions vary by metric and field; the audit needs metric-specific floor definitions to avoid apples-to-oranges verdicts.
community_default_belief: If a slice gap appears in the benchmark numbers, it reflects a real model property worth reporting.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Small slices make large gaps likely under the null; without power accounting, slice analysis is a noise amplifier.
fastest_falsification: If underpowered claims replicate at high rates on enlarged slices anyway, the power audit is solving a non-problem.

one_line: Split design is a measurable instrument property: splits along generative factors (photographer, session, site) predict deployment performance better than IID splits, by quantifiable margins.
problem: Benchmarks choose train/test splits by convention (random IID) without evidence about which split design makes the benchmark predictive of field performance.
core_hypothesis: There is a rankable hierarchy of split designs (random < temporal < collection-event < site/operator-disjoint) in terms of how well benchmark scores predict performance on genuinely fresh deployments, and the hierarchy is stable across task families.
falsifiable_prediction: For datasets with rich provenance metadata, building parallel benchmarks under each split design and correlating their scores with performance on held-out later-deployment data will reproduce the hypothesized hierarchy, with factor-disjoint splits showing the highest external correlation across task families.
why_important: Establishing split design as a validated engineering choice, with numbers, would end the practice of defaulting to IID splits that systematically overstate deployment readiness.
why_possibly_novel: Individual studies show IID-vs-OOD gaps; a controlled multi-design comparison measuring external predictive validity of the benchmark itself, as a design guideline, is hypothesized to be missing (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take 2 provenance-rich datasets; construct four split variants each; train/evaluate a fixed model zoo per variant; measure correlation of variant scores with true post-collection deployment data; compare across designs.
main_risk: Provenance metadata is rarely complete; missing factor labels blur the distinction between designs and dilute measured differences.
community_default_belief: Random splits are a neutral default; split design is a minor procedural detail.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Splits define what generalization the benchmark certifies; random splits certify interpolation within a collection event, which deployments never resemble.
fastest_falsification: If external correlations are indistinguishable across split designs on both datasets, split design is indeed a detail.

one_line: Single-collection-event benchmarks overestimate generalization because both splits share latent event factors (device, weather, operator); cross-event evaluation reveals the hidden gap.
problem: Most benchmarks are collected in one campaign, then split; the shared campaign context makes test performance an in-distribution measurement disguised as generalization.
core_hypothesis: A significant fraction of measured benchmark performance is attributable to latent collection-event factors common to train and test; scores drop materially when evaluation crosses event boundaries, and the drop size estimates the event-factor share of the headline score.
falsifiable_prediction: On datasets spanning multiple documented collection events, within-event test scores will exceed cross-event test scores consistently across models, and the gap will shrink toward zero as models are trained across more events, tracing an estimable event-factor curve.
why_important: Would quantify how much of published benchmark performance is campaign-specific inflation, recalibrating expectations for every single-campaign benchmark in use.
why_possibly_novel: Domain shift across datasets is well known; systematic decomposition of within-benchmark scores into task capability vs collection-event factor share, as an audit applicable to existing benchmarks, is hypothesized to be unformalized (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use 2 multi-event datasets; train models within events and across events; measure within/cross-event score gaps and their decay with event diversity in training.
main_risk: Event boundaries correlate with genuine content changes (different locations); attributing gaps to 'latent factors' vs 'content' needs matched-content controls.
community_default_belief: A held-out test split from the same collection measures how well the model generalizes.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The split holds out items, not the collection process; process factors leak across the split by construction.
fastest_falsification: If within-event and cross-event scores are equal on matched content, the event-factor share is nil.

one_line: Curator 'interestingness' filtering shifts all models' scores roughly uniformly: filtered and unfiltered test sets differ in difficulty but hypothesize no model-by-filter interaction.
problem: Test sets are heavily filtered by curators for quality and interest, prompting worry that filtering biases comparisons toward models resembling the curators' tastes.
core_hypothesis: Human curation filters act mainly on item difficulty and clarity, dimensions on which model scores move together, so filtering produces near-additive score shifts with negligible model-by-filter interaction for models above a basic competence threshold.
falsifiable_prediction: Scoring a diverse model set on filtered and unfiltered versions of the same item pool will show model-by-filter interaction terms statistically indistinguishable from zero in a two-way analysis, while the filter main effect is large; interaction will appear only for models below the competence threshold.
why_important: Would remove a standing objection to curated benchmarks and localize the real cost of curation to absolute-difficulty calibration, not comparative validity.
why_possibly_novel: Curation bias is often asserted; a factorial interaction test of curation effects on model comparisons, with a competence-threshold moderator, is hypothesized to be unrun (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Obtain a raw item pool plus curator decisions from one benchmark's construction (or re-curate a raw pool); evaluate ~15 models on both versions; fit the two-way model and test the interaction with pre-registered equivalence margins.
main_risk: Curator decisions may encode task semantics (excluding categories) rather than pure quality, in which case interactions are real and the null fails informatively.
community_default_belief: Curated test sets tilt comparisons toward whatever the curators found interesting, biasing model rankings.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Filtering along difficulty affects all competent models' scores in the same direction and roughly the same amount, leaving comparative structure intact.
fastest_falsification: A significant model-by-filter interaction among competent models on the first benchmark kills the equivalence.

one_line: Within-test-set near-duplicates act as hidden item weights, silently multiplying certain error modes; effective test size is materially below nominal size and computable.
problem: Duplicate detection is applied between train and test but rarely within test sets, where duplicate clusters distort both scores and uncertainty estimates in unmeasured ways.
core_hypothesis: Test sets contain embedding-detectable near-duplicate clusters that function as unintended importance weights on particular content, inflating or deflating models differentially by their performance on the duplicated content, and shrinking effective sample size below the nominal count by a computable factor.
falsifiable_prediction: Clustering test items by embedding similarity and re-scoring with cluster-deduplicated weights will change model scores beyond bootstrap noise on benchmarks with heavy duplication, reorder some adjacent pairs, and widen honest confidence intervals by the predicted effective-size correction.
why_important: Both scores and error bars on affected benchmarks are currently wrong in a correctable direction; a standard dedup-weighting pass would fix them without new data.
why_possibly_novel: Train-test leakage dominates the dedup literature; the within-test weighting mechanism and its effective-sample-size arithmetic for benchmark scoring are hypothesized to be unaddressed (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run embedding-based within-test clustering on 4 benchmarks; quantify duplication factors; re-score public models under cluster weights; compare score shifts and interval widths to predictions.
main_risk: Near-duplicate thresholds are arbitrary; results may be sensitive to clustering hyperparameters, requiring a threshold-sweep robustness report.
community_default_belief: Each test item contributes one independent observation; the nominal item count is the sample size.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Duplicated content contributes correlated observations, which is weighting by stealth; independence is an assumption the data visibly violates.
fastest_falsification: If cluster-weighted re-scoring never moves any benchmark's scores beyond noise, within-test duplication is immaterial in practice.

one_line: Minimal-pair test items (counterfactually edited originals) measure decision-boundary placement directly and predict robustness-intervention outcomes better than aggregate accuracy.
problem: Aggregate accuracy confounds where a model's decision boundary sits with how items happen to be distributed, so benchmarks cannot say what a model would do under small, meaningful input changes.
core_hypothesis: Test sets augmented with human-verified minimal pairs (originals plus single-factor counterfactual edits) yield a boundary-sensitivity score that dissociates from accuracy and better predicts which models benefit from robustness interventions and how they fail under distribution shift.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a model zoo, minimal-pair consistency and standard accuracy will decorrelate substantially, and minimal-pair scores will predict post-intervention (augmentation, adversarial training) improvement and OOD degradation better than accuracy does, on held-out models.
why_important: Adds a second, mechanistically meaningful axis to benchmarks at bounded annotation cost, informing intervention selection rather than just model ranking.
why_possibly_novel: Counterfactual augmentation exists for training and bias analysis; positioning minimal-pair consistency as a benchmark-level instrument validated against intervention outcomes is hypothesized to be undeveloped (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build minimal pairs for a subset of one benchmark (single-factor edits verified by annotators); evaluate a model zoo; test the dissociation and the intervention-prediction claims on held-out models.
main_risk: Constructing clean single-factor edits at scale is hard; edit artifacts could contaminate the boundary measurement.
community_default_belief: Higher benchmark accuracy implies more reliable behavior under small input perturbations.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Accuracy sums over items far from the boundary; two equal-accuracy models can place boundaries very differently, which only paired probes reveal.
fastest_falsification: If minimal-pair scores are collinear with accuracy across the zoo, the added axis is redundant.

one_line: Test-retest reliability—re-collecting a benchmark under its own protocol—bounds meaningful model differences, and several benchmark genres are hypothesized to have alarmingly low reliability.
problem: Psychometrics never reports an instrument without reliability coefficients, yet ML benchmarks report scores with no measurement of how much they would change if the benchmark were rebuilt to spec.
core_hypothesis: Benchmark genres differ systematically in test-retest reliability (human-preference evals lowest, procedurally verified tasks highest), and reliability measured once per genre transfers well enough to bound the interpretable score resolution of any benchmark in that genre.
falsifiable_prediction: Duplicate-collection experiments across genres will show a stable reliability ordering with human-preference benchmarks materially less reliable than verifiable-output benchmarks, and within-genre reliability predictions will transfer to new benchmarks within stated error.
why_important: Reliability coefficients would give every published score an honest resolution limit and expose genres where current leaderboard granularity is fiction.
why_possibly_novel: Isolated replication studies exist; genre-level reliability laws intended as reusable calibration constants for benchmark interpretation are hypothesized to be unestablished (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-collect miniature duplicates of one benchmark per genre (classification, extraction, preference) under original protocols; evaluate frozen models; compute genre reliability and test transfer to a second benchmark per genre.
main_risk: Miniature duplicates confound size with protocol; reliability at small n must be extrapolated carefully to full-size instruments.
community_default_belief: A benchmark score is a stable property of the model, reported to decimal places that reflect real precision.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The score is a joint property of model and one dataset realization; without retest data, its precision is unknown, not high.
fastest_falsification: If genre reliabilities are heterogeneous within genres or fail to transfer, no usable genre law exists.

one_line: Procedurally generated test sets with exact ground truth reproduce not only the rankings but the error-mode profiles obtained from human-annotated test sets within the same genre.
problem: Synthetic/procedural test data is distrusted for evaluation on the grounds that it misrepresents real-world difficulty, forcing continued reliance on expensive human annotation even where ground truth could be computed.
core_hypothesis: For genres where the task is well defined procedurally (geometry, counting, structured extraction, rendered scenes), procedurally generated test sets produce model orderings and confusion/error-mode profiles statistically equivalent to human-annotated counterparts, at a tiny fraction of cost.
falsifiable_prediction: Building matched procedural and human-annotated test sets for the same task specifications will show equivalence (within pre-registered margins) in both rankings and per-error-mode rates across a model zoo, with divergence limited to error modes involving real-world texture priors.
why_important: Where equivalence holds, communities can generate unbounded fresh uncontaminated test data forever, structurally solving saturation and contamination for those genres.
why_possibly_novel: Synthetic-to-real gaps are studied for training; the evaluation-side equivalence question, tested at the error-profile level rather than just rankings, is hypothesized to be open (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: For two procedural-friendly tasks, build both test-set types from one spec; evaluate ~12 models; compare rankings and error-mode distributions with equivalence tests.
main_risk: Procedural generators embed their own distributional choices; equivalence may reflect generator tuning to the human set rather than genre-level validity.
community_default_belief: Evaluation on synthetic data cannot substitute for evaluation on real annotated data.
why_that_may_be_wrong: For procedurally definable tasks, 'real' human annotation is itself an approximation of computable ground truth, and the approximation error may exceed the synthetic-real gap.
fastest_falsification: Ranking or error-profile divergence beyond margins on the first task pair breaks the equivalence.

one_line: Release benchmarks with a sealed ultra-hard stratum ('difficulty escrow') opened at saturation: an escrow sizing rule extends benchmark life predictably.
problem: Benchmarks saturate and die; successors take years to build and break comparability, leaving fields without discriminative instruments during transitions.
core_hypothesis: Holding back a top-difficulty stratum at release and unveiling it when the leaderboard nears the visible ceiling restores discriminative power on a comparable scale, and the escrow fraction needed can be sized at release from the difficulty distribution and forecast saturation dynamics.
falsifiable_prediction: Simulations on historical leaderboards (replaying with a synthetic escrow) will show that escrow release at the modeled saturation point restores rank resolution among the top cohort, and a pilot benchmark with a real escrow will reproduce the simulated resolution gain when opened.
why_important: A cheap release-time design decision (withhold a stratum) could roughly double the useful discriminative life of benchmarks, with continuity that successor benchmarks cannot offer.
why_possibly_novel: Hidden test sets are common for anti-cheating; deliberately difficulty-stratified escrows with a saturation-triggered release policy and a sizing rule are hypothesized to be undesigned (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Replay 3 finished leaderboards, synthetically withholding top-difficulty strata and 'releasing' at various times; measure restored resolution vs escrow size and timing; derive and sanity-check the sizing rule.
main_risk: Escrow items age (topical drift) and may leak; the design needs escrow-freshness checks at release time.
community_default_belief: When a benchmark saturates, the remedy is building a new benchmark.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Saturation is often a dynamic-range problem, not a content-exhaustion problem; reserved dynamic range can be banked at release and spent later.
fastest_falsification: If simulated escrow release fails to restore top-cohort resolution on historical replays, the mechanism is inert.

one_line: Cross-benchmark rank correlation decays smoothly with measurable distribution distance between benchmarks, giving a portability law for when a leaderboard winner transfers.
problem: Practitioners constantly extrapolate winners from one benchmark to adjacent settings with no quantitative guidance on when extrapolation holds.
core_hypothesis: The rank correlation between two benchmarks' leaderboards is a smooth decreasing function of an estimable distribution distance between them (over inputs and label semantics), fitted once per task family and usable to predict transfer of rankings to new settings.
falsifiable_prediction: Computing pairwise rank correlations and distribution distances across many benchmark pairs will show a monotone relationship with modest scatter within task families, and the fitted curve will predict held-out pairs' rank correlations within stated tolerance.
why_important: Would convert 'does the leaderboard apply to my problem?' from a judgment call into an estimate with error bars, guiding model selection outside benchmark conditions.
why_possibly_novel: Transferability of representations is studied; a portability law for rankings as a function of benchmark-distribution distance is hypothesized to be unfit (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble ~40 benchmark pairs across 3 task families with shared evaluated models; estimate distribution distances from embeddings and label maps; fit and cross-validate the decay curve.
main_risk: Distribution distance is hard to define across label spaces; a poor distance metric produces scatter that hides any law.
community_default_belief: Benchmark rankings either generalize or they don't; there is no quantitative in-between to estimate.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Transfer of orderings likely degrades continuously with distributional mismatch, like every other generalization phenomenon.
fastest_falsification: If rank correlation shows no monotone trend in distance within any family, the law is absent.

one_line: Battery-level benchmark performance is a strong single-factor predictor of deployment utility within a task family: the 'g-factor' reading of leaderboards is largely right.
problem: A growing critique holds that benchmark scores are laboratory artifacts disconnected from real-world usefulness, but the aggregate predictive validity of benchmark batteries is rarely measured against deployment outcomes.
core_hypothesis: A single latent factor extracted from a battery of benchmark scores predicts a large share of variance in deployment-relevant outcomes (user-rated task success, production regression rates) within a task family, vindicating benchmarks as coarse instruments even where individual benchmarks mislead.
falsifiable_prediction: Factor analysis of public benchmark batteries plus matched deployment outcome data (e.g., production A/B results, user success metrics where obtainable) will show the first factor explaining most benchmark variance and correlating strongly with deployment outcomes, exceeding any single benchmark's predictive power.
why_important: The field needs to know whether benchmark skepticism should target the instrument class or specific bad instruments; a validated g-factor would refocus criticism productively.
why_possibly_novel: Correlations among benchmarks are documented; the validation step connecting a battery factor to independent deployment outcomes, framed as rehabilitation of benchmark evidence, is hypothesized to be missing (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Partner with one production team (or use published A/B archives); assemble battery scores for the deployed model set; extract factors; test prediction of deployment outcomes against single-benchmark baselines.
main_risk: Deployment outcome data is scarce and selection-biased toward models that already passed benchmarks, restricting the observable range.
community_default_belief: Benchmark performance has decoupled from real-world usefulness; leaderboards no longer inform deployment decisions.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Individual benchmark pathologies can coexist with a robust common factor that tracks genuine capability, just as noisy tests can form reliable batteries.
fastest_falsification: If the battery factor predicts deployment outcomes no better than chance within the observed range, the rehabilitation collapses.

one_line: Benchmark-predicts-production claims are scale-confounded: within a compute/size class, benchmark deltas lose most of their power to predict production outcomes.
problem: Evidence that benchmarks predict downstream utility is typically computed across models of wildly different scales, so the correlation may be carried entirely by scale rather than by what benchmarks measure beyond it.
core_hypothesis: Conditioning on model scale (parameters, training compute) collapses most of the benchmark-production correlation; within-scale-class benchmark differences predict production outcomes only weakly, implying leaderboard gaps between same-scale models are poor deployment guides.
falsifiable_prediction: Partial-correlation analysis on model sets with known scale and production metrics will show the benchmark-production correlation dropping by a large fraction after scale conditioning, with within-class predictive power near the noise floor for most benchmark genres.
why_important: Deployment decisions among same-scale candidates are exactly where teams consult leaderboards; if that regime carries no signal, selection processes need different evidence.
why_possibly_novel: Scaling laws and benchmark correlations are both studied; the partial-correlation audit isolating benchmarks' scale-independent predictive content is hypothesized to be unperformed (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble ~30 models with public scale data, battery scores, and any production/user-preference outcomes; compute raw and scale-partialed correlations per benchmark genre.
main_risk: Scale proxies are imperfect for closed models, and production outcomes are noisy; both push toward false confirmation of the null.
community_default_belief: Benchmarks predict real-world performance, which is why leaderboards guide model selection.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Scale predicts both benchmark and production performance; benchmarks may be an expensive proxy for a number already on the model card.
fastest_falsification: If within-class benchmark deltas retain strong production prediction after conditioning, the confound claim fails.

one_line: Ensembling adds score but not rank information: leaderboards banning ensembles would produce the same method orderings, making ensemble arms races pure waste.
problem: Leaderboards permit ensembles, triggering costly ensemble arms races justified by the assumption that ensemble standings convey information single models do not.
core_hypothesis: Within a leaderboard, ensemble and best-single-model scores of the same team/method family are related by a near-uniform offset, so the ordering of method families is preserved when ensembles are excluded; ensemble standings are redundant with single-model standings.
falsifiable_prediction: On competition archives recording both single-model and ensemble submissions per team, the rank correlation between ensemble-based and single-model-based team orderings will be at the noise ceiling, and the ensemble gain will show low variance across teams relative to between-team gaps.
why_important: If confirmed, leaderboards can ban or separate ensembles without information loss, redirecting community compute from ensemble stacking to method development.
why_possibly_novel: Ensemble gains are well documented; the rank-redundancy claim—that ensembles never change who is ahead—tested across competition archives, is hypothesized to be unexamined (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Mine ~20 finished competitions with both submission types identifiable; compute ensemble-vs-single orderings and gain variance; test rank equivalence with pre-registered margins.
main_risk: Selection effects: teams that ensemble may differ systematically from teams that don't, biasing the offset-uniformity estimate.
community_default_belief: Ensemble results are part of the information a leaderboard provides; excluding them would change conclusions about which approach is best.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Ensemble gain is largely a mechanical variance-reduction available to everyone equally, so it cancels in comparisons.
fastest_falsification: If ensemble gains vary widely across teams and reorder standings in a material fraction of competitions, ensembles carry real rank information.

one_line: Mega-scores averaging many benchmarks are dominated by a few redundant clusters: the effective number of independent dimensions in popular suites is small and measurable.
problem: Aggregate suite scores are read as broad-capability summaries, but if constituent benchmarks are highly correlated, the average re-measures one latent factor while advertising breadth.
core_hypothesis: Factor and redundancy analysis of popular multi-benchmark suites will show a small effective dimensionality, with many benchmarks contributing near-zero marginal information to model discrimination, so suite averages can be replicated by a small weighted subset.
falsifiable_prediction: For widely used suites, a subset of a few benchmarks chosen by redundancy analysis will reproduce full-suite model rankings at the noise ceiling, and progress narratives based on suite averages will be shown to track single-factor movement in identified clusters.
why_important: Suite design and compute budgets should buy independent information; demonstrating redundancy would change which benchmarks suites include and how averages are interpreted.
why_possibly_novel: Benchmark correlation is noted anecdotally; a formal effective-dimensionality audit of named suites with minimal-subset reconstruction is hypothesized to be missing (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect per-benchmark scores of many public models on 2 popular suites; run factor analysis and subset-selection; validate ranking reconstruction on held-out models.
main_risk: Dimensionality depends on the model population; suites may be redundant for current models but discriminative for future ones.
community_default_belief: Averaging over many benchmarks yields a robust, broad measure of general capability.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Averaging correlated measurements narrows, rather than broadens, what is measured, while laundering the narrowness behind item count.
fastest_falsification: If no small subset reconstructs full-suite rankings, the suites are genuinely high-dimensional and the critique fails.

one_line: Rank-reversal frequency between two benchmarks is predictable from their per-item error correlation on a shared model set, yielding a cheap 'does this benchmark add information?' test.
problem: Suite maintainers add benchmarks without a quantitative criterion for whether a candidate benchmark will ever disagree with incumbents about model ordering.
core_hypothesis: The probability that two benchmarks reverse a model pair's order is a decreasing function of their per-item error correlation, well approximated by a two-parameter model, so a small pilot evaluation suffices to forecast a candidate benchmark's marginal ranking information.
falsifiable_prediction: Across benchmark pairs with shared model sets, observed rank-reversal frequencies will fit the correlation-based model within tolerance, and pilot-based forecasts (using a small model sample) will predict full-population reversal rates for held-out benchmark pairs.
why_important: Gives suite governance an admission test: benchmarks forecast to add no reversals are redundant regardless of topical novelty, saving evaluation compute and curation effort.
why_possibly_novel: Benchmark agreement is measured descriptively; an admission-test law with pilot-sized forecasting validated out-of-sample is hypothesized to be unavailable (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use public per-item results across ~30 benchmark pairs; fit the reversal model; test pilot forecasting with subsampled model sets on held-out pairs.
main_risk: Reversals concentrate among near-tied pairs where noise dominates; the model must separate informative reversals from tie-flickering.
community_default_belief: Whether a new benchmark adds value is a qualitative judgment about topical coverage.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Topical novelty without behavioral disagreement adds no measurement information; disagreement is forecastable from error statistics.
fastest_falsification: If reversal frequency is unrelated to error correlation across pairs, the admission test is baseless.

one_line: Decade-old 'obsolete' benchmarks retain rank validity: at matched compute, performance on small old benchmarks still correlates strongly with modern large-benchmark standings.
problem: Old benchmarks are declared obsolete and dropped from evaluation practice, but whether they stopped carrying comparative information—or merely stopped being fashionable—is untested.
core_hypothesis: The latent capability ordering measured by classic small benchmarks remains correlated with modern benchmark orderings at matched scale, so cheap legacy evaluations remain valid screening instruments, and their abandonment reflects saturation of absolute scores rather than loss of rank signal.
falsifiable_prediction: Evaluating a modern model zoo on classic benchmarks will show rank correlations with contemporary benchmark standings comparable to correlations among contemporary benchmarks themselves, once ceiling-compressed pairs (both models at ceiling) are excluded via psychometric correction.
why_important: Legacy benchmarks cost near-nothing to run; if they still rank correctly below the ceiling, they belong in continuous-integration screening where expensive modern suites are impractical.
why_possibly_novel: Nostalgic re-evaluations happen informally; a systematic rank-validity rehabilitation with ceiling correction and a screening-use recommendation is hypothesized to be unpublished (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run ~20 modern models on 5 classic benchmarks; compute ceiling-corrected rank correlations with modern suite standings; compare against inter-modern-benchmark correlations as the reference bar.
main_risk: Ceiling effects may be so severe that correction leaves too little variance, making the rehabilitation untestable rather than false.
community_default_belief: Saturated old benchmarks are useless for evaluating modern models.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Saturation compresses score range but need not destroy ordering below the ceiling; obsolescence conflates the two.
fastest_falsification: If ceiling-corrected legacy rankings decorrelate from modern standings while modern benchmarks inter-correlate, obsolescence is real.

one_line: Evaluation-harness harmonization matters below a capability threshold and stops mattering above it: rankings scramble for weak models but are protocol-invariant for strong ones.
problem: Harness details (prompt templates, extraction rules, stopping criteria) demonstrably move scores, prompting expensive harmonization efforts, but when protocol variance actually changes conclusions is uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: Protocol sensitivity is capability-dependent: below a threshold, models' scores under different harnesses reorder chaotically; above it, harness changes shift scores nearly uniformly, leaving rankings invariant—a two-regime structure with an estimable threshold.
falsifiable_prediction: Evaluating a capability-spanning model set under several harness configurations will show cross-harness rank correlation rising sharply with model capability and saturating at the noise ceiling beyond an identifiable threshold, reproducible across task genres.
why_important: Locates where harmonization investment pays off (comparisons involving weaker models) and where it is cosmetic (frontier comparisons), rationalizing community effort on evaluation infrastructure.
why_possibly_novel: Harness sensitivity is documented as a nuisance; the two-regime hypothesis with a capability threshold as the organizing law is hypothesized to be unproposed (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take ~20 models spanning capability; evaluate under 5 harness variants on 2 genres; plot cross-harness rank stability vs capability; test for the threshold and its cross-genre consistency.
main_risk: 'Capability' must be defined independently of the harnesses under test to avoid circularity; needs an external anchor measurement.
community_default_belief: Harness differences corrupt all cross-paper comparisons, so nothing is comparable until everyone adopts one harness.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Strong models may be robust to protocol variation in ways that make their comparisons naturally harness-invariant, confining the corruption to a regime the frontier has left.
fastest_falsification: If frontier-model rankings also scramble across harnesses, there is no safe regime and the equivalence fails.

one_line: LLM judges impose their training distribution as a hidden rubric: judge preference for models increases with the judged model's similarity to the judge's own family, on a measurable gradient.
problem: LLM-judged benchmarks now gatekeep model releases, but the judge is itself a model with a lineage, and the structure of its preferences across other models' lineages is unaudited.
core_hypothesis: Judge scores contain a similarity component: holding human-rated quality fixed, judge preference increases with representational/behavioral similarity between the judged model and the judge family, producing systematic leaderboard distortion beyond simple self-preference.
falsifiable_prediction: A judge-swap matrix (multiple judge families scoring the same response sets, anchored by human panels) will show a significant interaction between judge family and judged-model family, with preference gradients aligned to similarity measures, not just identity (self) effects.
why_important: If judges impose family-similarity gradients, entire leaderboard ecosystems inherit the dominant judge's lineage as an invisible standard, penalizing architectural diversity.
why_possibly_novel: Self-preference of judges is documented; the graded similarity effect across non-self families, quantified against human anchors and similarity measures, is hypothesized to be uncharacterized (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Score a fixed response corpus with 4 judge families; collect human panel ratings as anchor; regress judge-vs-human deviation on judged-to-judge similarity; test the gradient's significance.
main_risk: Similarity and genuine quality correlate if families share training data quality; needs careful anchoring and similarity measures independent of quality.
community_default_belief: A strong LLM judge is an approximately neutral grader whose errors are random with respect to model identity.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Judging is pattern-matching against the judge's learned distribution; models sampled from nearby distributions match better irrespective of quality.
fastest_falsification: If judge-vs-human deviations show no similarity structure beyond self-preference, the gradient claim fails.

one_line: Generated test items fail as benchmarks through distributional over-smoothness—missing rare configurations—not through per-item unrealism, and generator likelihood predicts the gap.
problem: Synthetic test sets are criticized for 'lack of realism', a vague diagnosis that gives generator builders no target and evaluators no correction handle.
core_hypothesis: The dominant defect of generated test sets is under-representation of low-likelihood configurations (tail smoothing), so models score higher on synthetic tests mainly because hard rare cases are missing, and the synthetic-real score gap is predictable from the generator's likelihood profile over real test items.
falsifiable_prediction: Binning real test items by generator likelihood will show the synthetic-real score gap concentrated in low-likelihood bins; reweighting synthetic sets toward the real likelihood profile will close most of the gap without improving per-item realism.
why_important: Redirects synthetic-eval engineering from photorealism/fluency (expensive, maybe irrelevant) to tail coverage (measurable, correctable), and yields a correction usable today.
why_possibly_novel: Synthetic-real gaps are documented; the mechanistic attribution to tail smoothing with a likelihood-based predictive and corrective handle is hypothesized to be untested (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: For one vision and one text task, score models on real and generated test sets; compute generator likelihoods over real items; test gap concentration in tails and the reweighting correction.
main_risk: Generator likelihood is hard to estimate for some architectures; a poor likelihood proxy would fail to reveal real concentration structure.
community_default_belief: Synthetic test data misleads because individual items are unrealistic.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Per-item realism can be high while the ensemble misses exactly the rare structures that separate strong from weak models; the defect is distributional, not itemwise.
fastest_falsification: If the synthetic-real gap is uniform across likelihood bins, tail smoothing is not the mechanism.

one_line: Disagreement-weighted triangulation across heterogeneous judge families approximates human-panel rankings better than any single judge, with a fittable judge-diversity value curve.
problem: LLM-judged evaluation inherits single-judge biases, but the community lacks a validated aggregation recipe or any quantification of how many and how different judges need to be.
core_hypothesis: Aggregating scores from judges of different lineages, weighting items by cross-judge disagreement (escalating disagreements to humans), converges toward human-panel rankings following a diminishing-returns curve in judge diversity, allowing principled judge-panel sizing under budget constraints.
falsifiable_prediction: On response corpora with human panel ground truth, judge-panel aggregates will show monotone ranking improvement with added lineage diversity (not mere count), with disagreement-escalation capturing most residual error at small human budgets, matching the fitted value curve on held-out corpora.
why_important: Would give evaluation platforms an evidence-based standard for judge panels, replacing ad hoc single-judge choices that currently encode invisible biases into public leaderboards.
why_possibly_novel: Judge ensembles are used informally; the diversity-value curve, disagreement-escalation design, and out-of-sample validation as a sizing methodology are hypothesized to be unformalized (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble 5 judge families and human panels on 2 response corpora; sweep panel compositions; fit ranking-error vs diversity curves; validate on a third corpus.
main_risk: Judge lineages share pretraining data heavily, capping achievable diversity and possibly flattening the value curve.
community_default_belief: Using the strongest available model as the single judge is the best evaluation practice.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Correlated bias, not judge weakness, is the binding error source, and strength does not decorrelate bias while diversity does.
fastest_falsification: If panels of diverse judges do no better than the best single judge against human anchors, triangulation is pointless.

one_line: Model-generated benchmark items resolve capability tiers but not within-tier order: synthetic evals separate weak from strong models, while fine-grained rankings require human-authored items.
problem: Communities increasingly generate benchmark items with LLMs for cost reasons, without knowing which evaluative questions generated items can and cannot answer.
core_hypothesis: Generated and human-authored item sets agree on coarse capability tiers (equivalence at the tier level) but diverge on within-tier orderings, because generated items under-sample the discriminative margins where near-peer models differ.
falsifiable_prediction: Evaluating a model zoo on matched generated and human-authored sets will show tier assignments (clusters separated by large gaps) statistically equivalent across set types, while within-tier rank correlations fall well below the bootstrap ceiling specifically for the generated sets.
why_important: Defines the legitimate scope of cheap synthetic evaluation—screening and tiering—while warning against using it to adjudicate close races, which is exactly where leaderboard stakes concentrate.
why_possibly_novel: Generated-vs-human eval comparisons exist at the aggregate-score level; the tier-vs-within-tier resolution decomposition as the organizing result is hypothesized to be unreported (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate and human-author item sets from one specification; evaluate ~20 models spanning tiers; compare tier equivalence and within-tier rank agreement with pre-registered margins.
main_risk: Tier boundaries are partly conventional; results may be sensitive to how tiers are defined, requiring gap-based rather than quantile-based definitions.
community_default_belief: With good prompting, LLM-generated benchmarks are interchangeable with human-authored ones.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Generation samples the generator's high-likelihood item space, which is systematically thin exactly at the hard margins that resolve near-peers.
fastest_falsification: If within-tier agreement matches human-set agreement, generated items are fully interchangeable and the limitation is imaginary.

one_line: Judge reliability decays on a predictable schedule as evaluated-model outputs saturate the public web and recirculate into judge training corpora.
problem: LLM judges are periodically retrained on web data that increasingly contains the outputs of the very model families they judge, but the reliability consequences of this circulation are unquantified.
core_hypothesis: Judge-vs-human agreement on responses from a given model family declines as a function of that family's output prevalence in the judge's training window, following a lagged dose-response driven by web publication and crawl schedules.
falsifiable_prediction: Comparing judge generations trained at different crawl cutoffs against fixed human-anchored response corpora will show family-specific agreement shifts that track the family's estimated web prevalence in each training window, with the predicted lag.
why_important: If judge quality drifts on a schedule set by web circulation, evaluation platforms need judge-version pinning and drift monitoring, or leaderboard time series confound model progress with judge drift.
why_possibly_novel: Model-output contamination of training corpora is discussed for capabilities; its specific effect on judge reliability as a lagged dose-response law is hypothesized to be unmeasured (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix human-rated response corpora from several model families; score them with successive judge versions of one lineage; estimate family web prevalence per training window from public crawl statistics; fit the lagged dose-response.
main_risk: Judge version differences bundle many changes (data, RLHF recipes); isolating the circulation effect may require controlled continued-pretraining rather than shipped versions.
community_default_belief: Newer, stronger judge versions grade more reliably across the board.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Newer judges have also ingested more evaluated-model output, and familiarity is not neutrality; reliability can fall for the most-circulated families even as general capability rises.
fastest_falsification: If agreement shifts across judge versions show no relationship to family prevalence estimates, the circulation mechanism is not operating measurably.

one_line: Static factuality benchmarks measure formatting compliance as much as knowledge: answer-format perturbations flip a large share of item outcomes while the underlying fact is held constant.
problem: Factuality and hallucination benchmarks score models on fixed probe phrasings and extraction rules, conflating knowing the fact with matching the expected answer shape.
core_hypothesis: A material fraction of pass/fail outcomes on static factuality benchmarks are format-determined: re-eliciting the same fact under semantically equivalent formats (cloze, multiple-choice, free-form, reversed) flips outcomes at rates far above what genuine knowledge variation could explain.
falsifiable_prediction: Item-level outcome agreement across equivalent formats will be weak for a large minority of items, format-flip rates will dwarf test-retest noise within a format, and aggregate benchmark rankings will shift measurably under format-marginalized scoring.
why_important: Hallucination metrics feed safety claims and deployment gates; if a chunk of the measurement is format compliance, both the absolute rates and some model comparisons are artifacts.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt sensitivity is well known in general; a factuality-specific decomposition into knowledge vs format components with format-marginalized re-scoring of named benchmark genres is hypothesized to be missing (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take one factuality benchmark; build four equivalent-format variants per item for a random subset; evaluate ~10 models; measure cross-format outcome agreement and re-rank under marginalized scoring.
main_risk: Constructing truly equivalent formats is delicate; difficulty drift between formats could mimic format sensitivity.
community_default_belief: A model that fails a factuality probe lacks or hallucinates the underlying knowledge.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The probe conflates retrieval with rendering; failure may occur in the rendering layer the benchmark never intended to test.
fastest_falsification: If outcomes agree strongly across formats, factuality benchmarks measure what they claim and the critique collapses.

one_line: Executable-specification item generators yield accuracy-vs-difficulty curves that are more stable model fingerprints than any static test score, and are contamination-proof by construction.
problem: Static test sets are consumable resources: once leaked or memorized they are spent, and their single-number outputs hide how performance varies with difficulty.
core_hypothesis: For tasks with programmatically verifiable ground truth, generators with controllable difficulty knobs produce per-model accuracy-vs-difficulty curves whose shape parameters are stable across generator seeds and re-generations, giving a reusable, unmemorizable measurement instrument with higher test-retest reliability than static scores.
falsifiable_prediction: Regenerating test batches from the same spec will reproduce each model's curve parameters within tight tolerance while static-subset scores fluctuate more; deliberately fine-tuning a model on one generated batch will not improve its curve on fresh batches, demonstrating contamination immunity.
why_important: A contamination-immune, difficulty-resolved instrument would end the arms race between benchmark secrecy and leakage for the substantial family of verifiable tasks.
why_possibly_novel: Procedural evaluation exists in niches; the claims that curve parameters beat static scores on reliability and that fine-tuning immunity is empirically demonstrable are hypothesized to be untested as a general methodology (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build generators with difficulty knobs for two verifiable tasks; evaluate ~10 models across regenerated batches; compare curve-parameter stability to static-score stability; run the fine-tune-on-batch contamination attack.
main_risk: Difficulty knobs may not span the difficulty axis real deployments care about, making stable curves stably irrelevant.
community_default_belief: Serious evaluation requires curated static test sets; generated items are for augmentation, not measurement.
why_that_may_be_wrong: For verifiable tasks, the specification is the benchmark; any static sample from it is strictly less information than the generator itself.
fastest_falsification: If curve parameters vary across regenerations as much as static scores, generators lose their claimed reliability advantage.

one_line: Micro-vs-macro aggregation silently decides winners on imbalanced benchmarks: a census will show undisclosed aggregation choices flipping a nontrivial share of published rankings.
problem: Leaderboards report single aggregate numbers whose micro/macro/weighted averaging convention is often undocumented, and the sensitivity of rankings to that convention is unaudited.
core_hypothesis: On benchmarks with skewed category or length distributions, a material fraction of adjacent leaderboard pairs reorder under the alternative aggregation convention, and the convention actually used is frequently unstated or inconsistent across papers citing the same benchmark.
falsifiable_prediction: Recomputing public leaderboards under both conventions will flip a nontrivial percentage of adjacent pairs beyond noise on imbalanced benchmarks, and a survey of papers will find a substantial share failing to state their convention or using different conventions for the same benchmark.
why_important: Ranking claims that depend on an undisclosed averaging switch are not reproducible science; making the sensitivity visible forces disclosure and dual reporting where it matters.
why_possibly_novel: Aggregation effects are textbook statistics; the empirical census quantifying how often the switch changes published conclusions, coupled with the disclosure audit, is hypothesized to be undone (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select 5 imbalanced benchmarks with per-item public results; recompute both conventions; count rank flips among adjacent pairs; audit 50 citing papers for convention disclosure.
main_risk: Per-item results are unavailable for many benchmarks, restricting the census to a possibly unrepresentative public-prediction subset.
community_default_belief: Aggregation convention is a technicality that does not affect who wins.
why_that_may_be_wrong: On skewed distributions, micro and macro averages weight the data differently enough to be different measurements; near-tied models can legitimately order both ways.
fastest_falsification: If flips are negligible even on the most imbalanced benchmarks, the convention truly is a technicality.

one_line: Tie-breaking and rounding conventions are immaterial on large-test benchmarks but material on small human-eval benchmarks, with the boundary computable from n and score granularity.
problem: Evaluation pedantry (rounding, tie handling, sample ordering) consumes reviewer and harness-builder attention without a principled account of when such details can and cannot change conclusions.
core_hypothesis: The maximum ranking perturbation inducible by convention choices is bounded by a function of test size and score granularity; above a computable threshold the conventions are provably immaterial, below it they are demonstrably capable of deciding winners.
falsifiable_prediction: Exhaustively sweeping convention combinations on benchmarks spanning sizes will show zero ranking changes above the computed threshold and reproducible convention-induced flips below it, matching the bound's predictions.
why_important: Lets the community stop arguing about conventions where they cannot matter and mandates convention pre-registration exactly where they can, mostly small human-preference evaluations.
why_possibly_novel: Individual convention bugs get noticed ad hoc; a general materiality bound with an empirical sweep validating both regimes is hypothesized to be unformalized (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement a convention-sweep harness; run on 6 benchmarks from tiny (hundreds of items) to large; record ranking perturbations; compare against the analytic bound.
main_risk: Exotic conventions outside the swept family could exceed the bound; the claim must be scoped to enumerated convention dimensions.
community_default_belief: Careful evaluation requires nailing down every scoring convention on every benchmark.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Convention effects are bounded by arithmetic; for most benchmark sizes the bound is far below the smallest gap anyone interprets.
fastest_falsification: A convention-induced rank flip on a benchmark above the threshold breaks the bound and the equivalence claim.

one_line: Pre-registered submission budgets (declared tuning runs, seeds, ablation intent) enable validity-weighted leaderboards that penalize invisible search, predictably reordering tuning-sensitive method classes.
problem: Leaderboards cannot distinguish a method that works robustly from one tuned exhaustively against the evaluation, because search effort is invisible in the submitted number.
core_hypothesis: Requiring declared budgets at submission and weighting scores by a validity factor (discounting for search intensity) produces rankings that better predict replication under fixed budgets, with reordering concentrated in method classes known for hyperparameter sensitivity.
falsifiable_prediction: In a controlled challenge where teams' true search logs are recorded, budget-weighted rankings will predict fixed-budget replication performance better than raw rankings, and the divergence between the two rankings will correlate with measured tuning sensitivity of the method class.
why_important: Aligns leaderboard incentives with robustness rather than search capacity, addressing a structural driver of irreproducible SOTA claims without banning tuning.
why_possibly_novel: Compute-adjusted comparisons are advocated in principle; an operational pre-registration mechanism with validity weights validated against replication outcomes is hypothesized to be unbuilt (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run a small community challenge with mandatory search logging; construct both rankings; replicate top methods under fixed budgets; compare predictive validity of the two rankings.
main_risk: Self-declared budgets invite misreporting; the mechanism needs audit hooks (seed pinning, log hashes) to be trustworthy at scale.
community_default_belief: The leaderboard number is the method's quality; how much search produced it is the submitter's private business.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Under selection pressure, the number measures the maximum of noisy draws, which grows with draw count; without budget accounting, leaderboards reward variance and search rather than mean quality.
fastest_falsification: If budget-weighted rankings predict fixed-budget replication no better than raw rankings, the weighting adds bureaucracy without validity.

one_line: Models have a measurable 'protocol gradient'—score sensitivity per unit change of evaluation parameters—and protocol-brittle models are identifiable before cross-harness disputes arise.
problem: Cross-paper score discrepancies trigger disputes that are resolved ad hoc, because nobody measures in advance how sensitive each model's scores are to evaluation-protocol parameters.
core_hypothesis: Score sensitivity to protocol parameters (resolution, context length, prompt format, decoding settings) is a stable per-model property: models cluster into robust and brittle groups, brittleness is consistent across benchmarks, and it predicts the magnitude of cross-harness score disagreements for that model.
falsifiable_prediction: Measuring finite-difference protocol gradients for ~20 models on 2 benchmarks will show high across-benchmark rank correlation of brittleness, and brittleness measured on one benchmark will predict the model's observed cross-harness variance on independent benchmarks.
why_important: A published protocol-gradient number per model would pre-explain most cross-paper discrepancies and identify which models' scores need protocol error bars.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt/protocol sensitivity is reported per benchmark; treating brittleness as a stable, transferable per-model property with predictive use is hypothesized to be unestablished (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define a protocol-parameter grid; evaluate models across it on two benchmarks; compute per-model gradients; test cross-benchmark stability and prediction of cross-harness variance from public reporting differences.
main_risk: Gradients may interact with parameter ranges (nonlinearity), making a single brittleness number too coarse; may need low-dimensional profiles instead.
community_default_belief: Score discrepancies across harnesses reflect sloppy evaluation practice by one of the parties.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Some models are intrinsically high-variance instruments under protocol change; discrepancies are then a model property, not an evaluator failure.
fastest_falsification: If brittleness rankings do not transfer across benchmarks, there is no stable property to publish.

one_line: Ritual 80/10/10 splitting is information-theoretically wasteful: optimal split proportions depend on dataset size and model-selection needs, and modern datasets should allocate far differently.
problem: Split proportions are inherited folklore from small-data eras; nobody derives them from the statistical requirements of the model-selection and reporting tasks the splits exist to serve.
core_hypothesis: The variance-optimal allocation among train/validation/test depends on dataset size, number of model-selection decisions, and required test precision; for large modern datasets the optimum shifts test and validation shares far below convention, while for small datasets convention under-allocates evaluation, and following the derived rule measurably improves selection reliability at fixed data budget.
falsifiable_prediction: Controlled experiments varying split allocations will show model-selection error and test-interval width tracking the derived optimum rather than convention, with conventional splits measurably suboptimal at both extremes of dataset size.
why_important: Split allocation touches every empirical study; even small systematic inefficiency multiplied across the field is a large waste, and small-data studies especially are under-powering their own conclusions by ritual.
why_possibly_novel: Optimal experiment design is classical; a practical, validated split-allocation rule for ML workflows spanning selection intensity and size regimes is hypothesized to be unadopted (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: On 3 datasets of different sizes, sweep split allocations; run standardized selection pipelines; measure selection regret and interval widths; compare empirical optima to the analytic rule.
main_risk: The optimum depends on selection-procedure details (how many candidates, early stopping), so one rule may fragment into workflow-specific variants.
community_default_belief: Standard split proportions are a reasonable default that does not materially affect research conclusions.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The statistical jobs of validation and test scale differently with data size and selection intensity; a fixed ratio cannot serve both regimes, and its error is directional and predictable.
fastest_falsification: If selection regret is flat across a wide allocation range on all sizes, the ritual is harmless and the rule unnecessary.

one_line: Reasonable metric variants agree about top models and disagree about the middle: metric debates matter for method development, not for SOTA claims.
problem: Communities burn effort litigating metric choices without knowing where in the ranking the choice actually changes conclusions.
core_hypothesis: Across reasonable metric variants for a task family, top-cohort rankings are invariant (equivalence within noise) while mid-tier rankings reorder substantially, because top models dominate on all facets the variants weight differently, whereas mid-tier models trade facets against each other.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-scoring public leaderboards under several accepted metric variants will show top-quintile rank correlations at the noise ceiling and mid-quintile correlations significantly below it, reproducibly across task families.
why_important: Locates the actual stakes of metric selection—development-time guidance for non-frontier methods—and defuses metric controversies about who is 'really' SOTA.
why_possibly_novel: Metric disagreement is documented per benchmark; the positional structure of that disagreement (top-invariant, middle-sensitive) as a general law is hypothesized to be unexamined (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 3 task families, re-score leaderboards under 3-4 accepted metric variants; compute positional rank-agreement profiles; test the top-vs-middle contrast with pre-registered thresholds.
main_risk: The definition of 'reasonable variants' is contestable; adversarially chosen metrics can break any invariance, so the variant set must be community-sourced.
community_default_belief: Choosing the right metric is decisive for correct benchmark conclusions at every level, including the top.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Pareto-dominant models win under any monotone facet weighting; metric choice only re-weights trade-offs that dominated models are making.
fastest_falsification: If top-cohort rankings flip across accepted variants in a task family, the top-invariance claim dies there.

one_line: Leaderboards as noisy channels: releasing rank-band feedback with calibrated score noise blocks adaptive overfitting while preserving the incentive gradient, testable in simulation and live challenges.
problem: Evaluation servers face a dilemma: precise public feedback enables holdout exploitation, while withholding feedback destroys the leaderboard's motivational and scientific function.
core_hypothesis: There is a feedback design (quantized rank bands plus noise calibrated to the test set's minimum detectable delta) that provably caps per-submission information leakage below exploitability thresholds while empirically preserving participant improvement rates and satisfaction relative to precise feedback.
falsifiable_prediction: In simulated adaptive attackers and a live A/B challenge, the noised-band design will reduce achievable holdout inflation to near zero where precise feedback permits measurable inflation, with no significant reduction in genuine (private-set) improvement across participant cohorts.
why_important: Would give evaluation platforms a principled dial replacing today's ad hoc submission limits, protecting benchmark longevity without chilling participation.
why_possibly_novel: Adaptive-analysis theory proposes noise mechanisms abstractly; an end-to-end leaderboard design validated for both leakage and incentive preservation in live use is hypothesized to be unbuilt (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement attacker simulations against both feedback designs; then run a two-arm live challenge with matched tasks; compare holdout inflation and participant progress metrics between arms.
main_risk: Noise erodes trust: participants may perceive banded feedback as unfair or buggy, harming adoption regardless of statistical merits.
community_default_belief: Leaderboards must report precise scores to be useful; anti-gaming measures mean submission caps.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The scientifically meaningful signal is already coarser than reported precision; reporting only the meaningful granularity costs nothing real while starving attackers.
fastest_falsification: If simulated attackers inflate holdout scores through the noised bands nearly as well as through precise feedback, the channel design fails.

one_line: Benchmarks mutate silently after release (takedowns, link rot, re-encodes): the 'same benchmark' cited across years is materially different data, confounding longitudinal claims.
problem: Datasets distributed via URLs and periodic re-hosting change composition over time, yet papers treat benchmark names as referring to fixed objects when comparing against prior years' numbers.
core_hypothesis: For URL-distributed and re-hosted benchmarks, item-level composition drift across years is large enough that a measurable share of reported longitudinal 'progress' or 'regression' is attributable to evaluating on different effective datasets, not different models.
falsifiable_prediction: Reconstructing dated snapshots of several benchmarks (from archives, checksums, and mirrors) and evaluating fixed frozen models across snapshots will show score drift comparable to typical published year-over-year method gains on at least some widely used benchmarks.
why_important: Longitudinal comparisons underpin narratives of field progress; if the measuring stick drifts, some of those narratives need correction, and citation practices need snapshot identifiers.
why_possibly_novel: Link rot is documented bibliometrically; the quantitative connection from composition drift to confounded model-progress claims, measured with frozen models across reconstructed snapshots, is hypothesized to be new (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Reconstruct 3+ dated snapshots for 3 URL-distributed benchmarks; evaluate 5 frozen models per snapshot; compare cross-snapshot score drift to published method-gain magnitudes on those benchmarks.
main_risk: Snapshot reconstruction is imperfect; unrecoverable items force approximations that could overstate or understate drift.
community_default_belief: A named benchmark is a fixed reference object; scores on it from different years are directly comparable.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The name persists while the bytes do not; distribution infrastructure quietly rewrites the dataset under the citation.
fastest_falsification: If frozen-model scores are stable across reconstructed snapshots for all examined benchmarks, silent mutation is not a material confound.

one_line: Dataset item decay follows a fittable survival curve, and decay is content-biased: takedown-prone categories vanish faster, predictably distorting composition over a benchmark's life.
problem: Benchmarks referencing external content lose items continuously, but the rate, shape, and content bias of that loss have never been modeled as the predictable process it is.
core_hypothesis: Item survival in URL-referencing datasets follows a mixture survival model with covariates (host type, content category, license status), and because hazard rates differ by content type, surviving subsets drift in composition along a predictable trajectory rather than shrinking uniformly.
falsifiable_prediction: Fitting survival models to recoverability data across several aged datasets will show strong covariate effects (e.g., personal-media content decaying faster than institutional content), and composition drift of survivors will match the hazard model's forecast at later checkpoints.
why_important: Enables maintainers to forecast benchmark decay, schedule preservation interventions before critical strata vanish, and correct scores for known composition drift retroactively.
why_possibly_novel: Link rot rates are reported as aggregates; covariate-structured survival modeling with composition-drift forecasting for benchmark integrity is hypothesized to be unattempted (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Probe recoverability of items in 4 aged URL-based datasets; fit covariate survival models; hold out the newest recoverability wave to test drift forecasts.
main_risk: Recoverability probing itself is noisy (mirrors, geo-blocks); measurement error in the outcome variable could wash out covariate structure.
community_default_belief: Dataset decay is random attrition that shrinks the sample but leaves it representative.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Deletion is behavior, not chance: content types face different legal, commercial, and personal takedown pressures, so attrition is a biased filter.
fastest_falsification: If survival curves show no covariate structure across datasets, decay is effectively random and the drift forecasts are baseless.

one_line: Content-addressed benchmark releases (per-item hashes plus scoring manifests) would make scores byte-reproducible; an audit will show current exact-reproduction attempts failing at high rates for fixable reasons.
problem: Reproducing a published benchmark score exactly—same data, same scoring—routinely fails for mundane infrastructural reasons, but the failure rate and its causes have not been measured, and no standard prevents them.
