core_hypothesis: A release standard of content-addressed items, pinned preprocessing, and executable scoring manifests eliminates a measurable class of reproduction failures; an audit of current practice will find exact reproduction failing for a majority of sampled benchmark results, with causes concentrated in a short fixable taxonomy (version ambiguity, preprocessing divergence, harness defaults).
falsifiable_prediction: Attempting exact reproduction of ~30 published benchmark numbers will fail at first attempt in most cases with causes classifiable into the proposed taxonomy, and re-running the same studies under a content-addressed pilot standard will succeed at a far higher rate.
why_important: Score reproducibility is the floor under all benchmark-based claims; quantifying the current failure rate and demonstrating the fix would move the field's infrastructure standards.
why_possibly_novel: Reproducibility crises are discussed at the finding level; the byte-level score-reproduction failure rate and a validated content-addressing remedy for benchmarks specifically are hypothesized to be unmeasured (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sample 30 published results with released code/data; attempt exact reproduction; classify failures; package the same benchmarks under the pilot standard and measure the reproduction rate improvement.
main_risk: Selection bias toward reproducible-looking papers; the audit sample must be drawn systematically to support rate claims.
community_default_belief: If code and data are released, published benchmark numbers are reproducible.
why_that_may_be_wrong: 'The data' is not a fixed object and 'the scoring' is not a fixed procedure; both drift under unversioned infrastructure even with good intentions.
fastest_falsification: If most sampled results reproduce exactly on first attempt, the infrastructure problem is smaller than claimed.

one_line: The field's conclusions are robust to removing any single contested dataset: retraining without it changes absolute scores but is hypothesized to preserve capability rankings.
problem: Dataset retractions and licensing disputes trigger fears that models and conclusions built on contested corpora are invalidated, but the actual sensitivity of conclusions to single-corpus removal is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: Modern training pipelines draw from redundant data sources, so ablating any single contested dataset from pretraining changes downstream benchmark scores by small absolute margins and preserves cross-model and cross-method rankings within noise.
falsifiable_prediction: Controlled retrain-with-ablation experiments at moderate scale will show single-corpus removal shifting downstream scores by less than typical seed variance for most corpus-benchmark pairs, with rank preservation across method comparisons, except when the removed corpus uniquely covers a niche capability.
why_important: Would let the community handle data governance disputes (retractions, licensing) without existential claims about invalidated science, and would identify the rare genuinely load-bearing corpora deserving special stewardship.
why_possibly_novel: Data ablations exist for capability attribution; framing them as robustness certificates for the field's comparative conclusions under dataset retraction is hypothesized to be new (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: At an affordable scale, pretrain matched models with and without each of 3 contested corpora; evaluate on a benchmark battery; compare deltas to seed-variance bands and test rank preservation.
main_risk: Effects may be scale-dependent: negligible at experimental scale but material at frontier scale, limiting the certificate's reach.
community_default_belief: Removing a major dataset from training would meaningfully change what models can do and which methods look best.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Web-scale corpora overlap enormously in content; any single source's unique contribution may be marginal redundancy, not load-bearing capability.
fastest_falsification: If ablating a contested corpus shifts scores well beyond seed variance and reorders methods, single-source dependence is real.

one_line: Documentation quality and label quality are uncorrelated across public datasets: datasheets signal compliance effort, not data integrity, so documentation-based dataset selection is unfounded.
problem: Practitioners and reviewers increasingly use documentation artifacts (datasheets, cards) as a proxy for dataset quality when selecting benchmarks, without evidence the proxy tracks measurable integrity.
core_hypothesis: Because documentation is produced by compliance and publication incentives while label integrity is produced by curation investment, the two are driven by different processes and will show near-zero correlation across public datasets once venue and recency are controlled.
falsifiable_prediction: Scoring documentation completeness and independently auditing label error rates on matched samples across ~40 public datasets will yield a correlation statistically indistinguishable from zero after controls, with high-documentation/high-error and low-documentation/low-error quadrants both well populated.
why_important: If the proxy fails, dataset governance needs direct integrity measurement (audit samples) rather than paperwork requirements, redirecting policy effort from documentation mandates to verification infrastructure.
why_possibly_novel: Datasheet adoption is studied descriptively; the empirical validity test of documentation as an integrity proxy is hypothesized to be unrun (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define a documentation completeness rubric; sample and expert-audit ~100 items per dataset for label errors; estimate the controlled correlation with pre-registered equivalence margins.
main_risk: Label-error auditing at fixed sample size has wide intervals for low-error datasets, limiting power to distinguish small true correlations from zero.
community_default_belief: Well-documented datasets are better-quality datasets; documentation requirements raise data standards.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Documentation measures the team's writing and compliance capacity; label quality measures their annotation pipeline; nothing forces these to covary.
fastest_falsification: A robust positive correlation surviving controls would validate the proxy and kill the null.

one_line: Dataset adoption follows early-citation cascades, not measured quality: matched-quality later datasets show systematically lower adoption, quantifying scientific lock-in in benchmark choice.
problem: The community treats a benchmark's popularity as evidence of fitness, but adoption dynamics may be dominated by first-mover network effects that are independent of measurable quality.
core_hypothesis: Controlling for measurable quality attributes (size, label integrity, task coverage, documentation), a dataset's long-run adoption is predicted primarily by its early citation trajectory and toolchain integration timing, with quality attributes contributing marginal predictive power—implying benchmark monopolies are path-dependent accidents.
falsifiable_prediction: Bibliometric survival analysis on cohorts of same-task datasets will show early-window citation velocity and framework-integration dates dominating quality covariates in predicting adoption, and identifiable matched pairs where the objectively weaker (by audit) dataset achieved dominance.
why_important: If benchmark monopolies are path accidents, the field's research directions are steered by history rather than merit, strengthening the case for deliberate benchmark governance and rotation.
why_possibly_novel: Citation cascades are studied in science-of-science; applying the framework to benchmark adoption with independent quality audits as covariates is hypothesized to be undone (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble same-task dataset cohorts; collect adoption time series, integration dates, and audit-based quality scores; fit adoption models; compare predictive contributions.
main_risk: Quality is multi-dimensional and partially unobservable; residual confounding could masquerade as path dependence.
community_default_belief: The most-used benchmarks earned their position by being the best available instruments.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Adoption compounds through citation norms and tooling defaults, mechanisms indifferent to instrument quality after the initial seeding.
fastest_falsification: If quality covariates dominate early-trajectory variables in adoption models, popularity does track merit and the debunk fails.

one_line: A version-pinning registry that auto-publishes same-model score diffs across dataset versions would separate model progress from data drift; piloting it will reveal how much published 'progress' is drift.
problem: When benchmarks version (fixes, expansions, re-hosting), the community keeps citing one name, and no infrastructure tracks how scores move for fixed models across versions.
core_hypothesis: Routine publication of frozen-model score diffs across dataset versions (a 'data changelog with scores') makes drift visible and correctable, and retroactive application to existing version histories will attribute a measurable fraction of cited cross-year improvements to version changes rather than modeling advances.
falsifiable_prediction: For benchmarks with recoverable version histories, frozen-model diffs will be nonzero and occasionally comparable to published method gains; prospective operation of the registry on active benchmarks will catch at least one version-induced score shift misattributable to model change within its first year.
why_important: Provides the missing observability layer for dataset evolution, protecting longitudinal claims and enabling honest version citation at near-zero marginal cost per release.
why_possibly_novel: Versioning tools exist for data engineering; the score-diff publication norm as benchmark-integrity infrastructure, with retroactive drift attribution, is hypothesized to be unimplemented (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Reconstruct version pairs for 4 benchmarks; run 5 frozen models on each version; publish diff tables; compare drift magnitudes against published gains citing those benchmarks across the same period.
main_risk: Version reconstruction may be impossible for exactly the benchmarks that drifted most, biasing measured drift downward.
community_default_belief: Dataset version changes are minor housekeeping that does not affect reported results.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Fixes and expansions change item composition and difficulty; without measurement, 'minor' is an assumption, not a fact.
fastest_falsification: If frozen-model diffs across all recoverable version pairs are negligible, drift is indeed housekeeping and the registry is unneeded.

one_line: Fitting item-response models to public leaderboard matrices identifies low-discrimination items whose removal shrinks benchmarks substantially with zero ranking loss.
problem: Benchmarks carry thousands of items that may contribute nothing to distinguishing models, inflating evaluation cost and diluting signal, but no standard procedure prunes them.
core_hypothesis: Two-parameter IRT fits on model-by-item response matrices will show a large mass of items with near-zero discrimination for the current model population; pruning them yields a much smaller core benchmark whose rankings and confidence intervals match the full set.
falsifiable_prediction: On several benchmarks with public per-item results, the pruned core (retaining a minority of items) will reproduce full-benchmark rankings at the bootstrap ceiling for held-out models, while equal-size random subsets will not.
why_important: Evaluation compute is a growing bottleneck; validated benchmark compression would cut costs across the field and sharpen the interpretation of what benchmarks measure.
why_possibly_novel: IRT has been applied descriptively to some leaderboards; a validated compression procedure with held-out ranking guarantees, offered as standard benchmark maintenance, is hypothesized to be unestablished (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fit IRT on 3 leaderboard matrices; prune by discrimination; evaluate ranking fidelity on held-out models vs random-subset baselines across compression levels.
main_risk: Items uninformative for current models may discriminate future models; pruning must retain a difficulty-reserve stratum or the core ages badly.
community_default_belief: Bigger test sets are better benchmarks, and every item contributes to the measurement.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Measurement value is concentrated in items whose difficulty sits near model abilities; the rest add cost and noise, not information.
fastest_falsification: If pruned cores lose ranking fidelity on held-out models at any meaningful compression, the compression claim fails.

one_line: Item difficulty is model-era-invariant to first order: difficulty estimated from one architecture generation predicts the next generation's per-item error ordering with high fidelity.
problem: Whether 'difficulty' is a property of items or an interaction between items and model families determines if any difficulty-based benchmark engineering can survive model evolution, but the invariance has not been measured across eras.
core_hypothesis: Per-item difficulty orderings are dominated by item-intrinsic factors, so difficulty estimates transfer across architecture eras with high rank correlation, while a small residual component—era-inconsistent items—captures genuine paradigm differences.
falsifiable_prediction: Splitting leaderboard archives by era and cross-predicting per-item error rates will show high transfer correlations across all era pairs, with the residual set small, stable in size, and enriched for identifiable item features rather than random.
why_important: Era-invariance underwrites every difficulty-based design tool (adaptive testing, pruning, stratified release); its measured strength and failure set define how durable those tools are.
why_possibly_novel: Difficulty transfer is assumed implicitly by IRT applications; the explicit cross-era invariance measurement with residual characterization is hypothesized to be unreported (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Partition archived submissions of 2 long-lived leaderboards into eras; estimate per-item difficulty within each; compute cross-era prediction fidelity; characterize the inconsistent residual items.
main_risk: Era boundaries within one benchmark's archive may not capture true paradigm shifts if the benchmark's model population lags the frontier.
community_default_belief: New model paradigms redefine what is hard, so old difficulty estimates are obsolete on arrival.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Most difficulty comes from item properties (ambiguity, rarity, required precision) that no paradigm dissolves; paradigms move the ability scale more than the item ordering.
fastest_falsification: Low cross-era transfer correlation on the first archive examined refutes first-order invariance.

one_line: Era-inconsistent items—those whose difficulty shifts between model generations—form a compact, automatically minable probe set that reveals what actually changed between paradigms.
problem: Claims about what new model generations 'really improved' are argued from anecdotes and aggregate scores, neither of which localizes the change.
core_hypothesis: Items whose difficulty ranking moves sharply between eras are concentrated probes of the capabilities that changed; clustering these items by feature yields an interpretable, benchmark-derived map of inter-generational capability deltas that aggregate scores cannot provide.
falsifiable_prediction: Era-inconsistent items mined from leaderboard archives will cluster into a small number of coherent feature groups (validated by human labeling), and held-out models from each era will show the predicted group-wise performance signature, unlike era-consistent control items.
why_important: Provides an automatic, reusable method for characterizing capability shifts—useful for benchmark refresh design, model documentation, and tracking what progress consists of.
why_possibly_novel: Difficulty shift analysis exists in psychometrics as item drift detection; using drift items as capability-delta probes for ML paradigm comparisons is hypothesized to be unpracticed (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Mine era-inconsistent items from one archive; cluster and human-label them; validate signatures on held-out era-representative models against control items.
main_risk: Inconsistent items may be dominated by label errors and protocol artifacts rather than capability shifts; needs an artifact-screening pass.
community_default_belief: Aggregate score gains tell us how much better new models are; understanding what changed requires bespoke probing studies.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The benchmark archive already contains a natural experiment across eras; its item-level residuals encode the 'what' that aggregates average away.
fastest_falsification: If era-inconsistent items fail to cluster coherently or signatures don't validate on held-out models, they are noise, not probes.

one_line: Claimed capability gains on several benchmark genres concentrate on low-discrimination and disputed items: IRT-rescored deltas will shrink headline improvements measurably.
problem: Method papers report aggregate deltas without item-level accounting, so gains earned on psychometrically worthless items (no discrimination, disputed labels) count the same as gains on sound items.
core_hypothesis: For a measurable share of recent claimed improvements, the delta concentrates on items that IRT analysis flags as low-discrimination or that audits flag as label-disputed, so information-weighted rescoring shrinks those deltas toward noise while leaving genuinely broad improvements intact.
falsifiable_prediction: Recomputing published deltas under discrimination-weighted scoring on benchmarks with per-item public results will shrink a nontrivial fraction of claimed gains below the significance threshold, while a control set of landmark improvements survives reweighting.
why_important: Would give reviewers and readers a cheap validity filter for improvement claims and pressure benchmark reporting toward information-weighted metrics.
why_possibly_novel: IRT weighting exists in testing science; auditing the ML literature's claimed deltas through that lens, with a landmark-control design, is hypothesized to be undone (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select ~20 claimed improvements with public per-item outputs; fit IRT on the underlying leaderboards; recompute deltas under discrimination weighting; compare shrinkage between recent marginal claims and landmark controls.
main_risk: Discrimination estimates depend on the model population used for fitting; unstable fits could unfairly shrink legitimate gains on hard novel items.
community_default_belief: A statistically significant aggregate delta on a standard benchmark is evidence of method improvement.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Aggregates launder where the gain came from; deltas earned on measurement-dead items are significant arithmetic, not significant capability.
fastest_falsification: If reweighting leaves recent marginal claims as intact as landmarks, gains are not concentrated on worthless items.

one_line: Refresh benchmarks at the ability frontier: adding items where top models sit near 50% success maximizes information gain per item and predictably multiplies discriminative lifetime.
problem: Benchmark refreshes add items by topical coverage or convenience, without targeting the difficulty region where new items actually discriminate among current top models.
core_hypothesis: An item-addition policy targeting the current top cohort's ability frontier (predicted success near 50%) yields several times more ranking information per added item than coverage-driven addition, and a refresh schedule following this policy extends a benchmark's discriminative lifetime in a predictable, simulation-matched way.
falsifiable_prediction: In leaderboard replays and one live refresh, frontier-targeted item batches will restore top-cohort rank resolution per item at multiples of the rate of coverage-matched control batches, matching information-theoretic predictions within tolerance.
why_important: Refresh budgets are scarce; a validated targeting policy converts the same annotation spend into much longer benchmark usefulness, directly countering saturation.
why_possibly_novel: Adaptive item banking is standard psychometrics; a refresh policy for ML benchmarks with live validation and lifetime accounting is hypothesized to be unimplemented (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Replay 2 saturated leaderboards adding synthetic item batches at various difficulty targets; measure resolution restoration per item; run one modest live refresh with frontier vs coverage arms.
main_risk: Frontier targeting requires predicting item difficulty pre-annotation, which is itself noisy; policy value degrades with difficulty-prediction error.
community_default_belief: Benchmark refreshes should prioritize topical coverage and realism of new items.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Coverage without discriminative placement adds items models already pass or uniformly fail, which cost the same to build and measure nothing about the frontier.
fastest_falsification: If frontier-targeted batches restore resolution no faster than coverage batches in replays, the targeting policy is worthless.

one_line: Human response time and model difficulty are near-orthogonal on several benchmark genres: 'hard for humans' curation does not produce model-discriminative items.
problem: Benchmark builders curate 'challenging' items using human effort signals (response time, perceived difficulty), assuming human and model difficulty align.
core_hypothesis: Across several genres, per-item human response time and model error rates correlate weakly or not at all, because human difficulty is driven by search and working-memory load while model difficulty is driven by distributional rarity and precision demands—different axes that curation conflates.
falsifiable_prediction: Collecting human response times and model error rates on shared item sets will yield correlations near zero (within pre-registered bounds) for genres like perception and retrieval-style QA, with alignment appearing only in multi-step reasoning genres.
why_important: If the axes are orthogonal, human-effort-based curation wastes budget and systematically fails to challenge models, explaining why some 'hard' benchmarks saturate immediately; curation should use model-based difficulty prediction instead.
why_possibly_novel: Scattered observations of human-model difficulty mismatch exist; a systematic multi-genre orthogonality measurement with curation-policy implications is hypothesized to be missing (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 3 genres, collect timed human performance on ~300 items each; evaluate a model zoo on the same items; estimate correlations with genre moderators; pre-register orthogonality bounds.
main_risk: Response time is a noisy difficulty proxy contaminated by interface and motivation effects; needs within-subject designs and attention controls.
community_default_belief: Items that challenge humans will challenge models; human difficulty is a sound curation signal for hard benchmarks.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Model failure concentrates where training distributions are thin, which has no reason to coincide with what strains human cognition.
fastest_falsification: Strong human-model difficulty correlations across genres would validate current curation and kill the orthogonality claim.

one_line: Answer-format psychometrics (guessing floors, slip ceilings) compress scores format-specifically, so cross-format capability comparisons are biased in computable, correctable directions.
problem: Benchmarks mix answer formats (multiple choice, free-form, cloze) and compare scores across them as if format were neutral, ignoring that formats impose different guessing floors and slip rates.
core_hypothesis: Each answer format induces characteristic guessing (c) and slip (d) parameters; uncorrected scores therefore compress differently by format, and applying format-specific psychometric correction changes cross-format conclusions (e.g., modality gaps, task-family comparisons) in directions predictable from the c/d estimates alone.
falsifiable_prediction: Estimating c/d per format from response data and re-scoring will show systematic, format-consistent corrections across benchmarks, with cross-format capability gaps shifting in the direction and approximate magnitude predicted by the fitted parameters.
why_important: Cross-format comparisons underpin claims about what models are 'better at'; format-induced compression is a lurking artifact with an off-the-shelf correction the field is not applying.
why_possibly_novel: Guessing correction is ancient psychometrics; measuring format-specific c/d for ML benchmarks and demonstrating that corrections overturn published cross-format conclusions is hypothesized to be untried (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: For matched content administered in 3 formats to the same model zoo, fit 4-parameter IRT per format; compare corrected vs raw cross-format gaps; validate the correction's predictive consistency across two benchmarks.
main_risk: Formats also change the task cognitively, not just psychometrically; correction may under- or over-attribute differences to floor/ceiling artifacts.
community_default_belief: Score differences between formats reflect capability differences on the underlying content.
why_that_may_be_wrong: A quarter of a multiple-choice score can be luck and a slice of free-form failure can be formatting slips; the arithmetic of floors and ceilings distorts comparisons before capability enters.
fastest_falsification: If fitted c/d parameters vary as much within formats as between them, format psychometrics have no systematic structure to correct.

one_line: Report IRT ability with standard errors instead of raw accuracy: ability estimates are invariant across item subsets and benchmark versions where raw scores are not, making them the correct exchange currency.
problem: Raw accuracy depends on the difficulty composition of whichever items happened to be used, so scores are incomparable across benchmark versions, subsets, and adaptive evaluations—yet raw accuracy remains the universal reporting standard.
core_hypothesis: Latent ability estimates from calibrated item pools are approximately invariant to item-subset choice, so ability-based reporting (with standard errors) enables valid comparison across versions, subsets, and adaptive administrations, and its adoption cost is repaid by measurable reductions in cross-version comparison error.
falsifiable_prediction: Evaluating models on disjoint calibrated subsets of the same pool will show ability estimates agreeing within their standard errors while raw accuracies diverge widely; cross-version model comparisons via ability will match full-pool ground truth far better than via raw scores.
why_important: The field's core reporting unit is composition-dependent; switching to an invariant unit would fix a foundational comparability defect affecting every leaderboard and paper.
why_possibly_novel: Ability metrics are standard in psychometrics; demonstrating their invariance advantage on ML benchmarks and proposing the reporting migration path is hypothesized to be unargued in ML venues (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Calibrate an item pool from public leaderboard data; evaluate held-out models on disjoint subsets; compare invariance of ability vs raw accuracy; quantify cross-version comparison error under both units.
main_risk: Ability estimates inherit IRT model misspecification; multidimensional tasks may violate the unidimensional ability assumption visibly.
community_default_belief: Percent-correct on the benchmark is the natural and sufficient unit for reporting model performance.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Percent-correct is a property of the item sample, not the model; psychometrics abandoned it for exactly this reason a century ago.
fastest_falsification: If ability estimates disagree across subsets as much as raw scores do, the invariance advantage is illusory for ML benchmarks.

one_line: Published human baselines are collected under low-incentive, unstandardized conditions and systematically underestimate motivated-expert performance, inflating 'superhuman' claims.
problem: Model-versus-human claims hinge on human baseline numbers gathered as afterthoughts—varying incentives, time limits, expertise, and instructions—yet these numbers gatekeep major capability announcements.
core_hypothesis: Re-measuring human baselines under standardized high-incentive protocols (calibrated payment, adequate time, qualified participants, practice items) will raise measured human performance materially on a substantial fraction of benchmarks currently claiming model-over-human superiority, revising some superiority claims to parity or reversal.
falsifiable_prediction: On a sample of benchmarks with published human baselines and 'superhuman' model claims, incentive-controlled re-measurement will raise human scores by margins exceeding the model-human gap in a nontrivial share of cases, with the raise predictable from the original protocol's incentive deficits.
why_important: Superhuman claims shape policy, investment, and deployment decisions; if the human reference is soft, those decisions rest on measurement artifacts.
why_possibly_novel: Individual baseline critiques exist; a systematic incentive-controlled re-measurement program quantifying how much baseline softness inflates superiority claims is hypothesized to be unexecuted (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select 6 benchmarks with superhuman claims; re-measure baselines under a standardized high-incentive protocol with documented participant qualification; compare revised gaps to published gaps.
main_risk: Expert recruitment and incentive design are costly, and 'motivated expert' is itself a choice that critics can dispute as an unfair goalpost move.
community_default_belief: Published human baselines are reasonable estimates of human ability on the task.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Baseline humans were often unpaid, untrained, time-pressured, or unqualified; the number measures the protocol's carelessness, not human capability.
fastest_falsification: If high-incentive re-measurement moves baselines negligibly across the sample, published baselines were sound and the critique fails.

one_line: Where humans are presumed superior (commonsense, cluttered perception), realistic-condition human measurement is hypothesized to fall below the idealized reference, understating current model standing.
problem: Claims that models still lag humans on 'easy for humans' tasks often rest on idealized human references (unlimited time, best-case attention) rather than measured performance under realistic conditions.
core_hypothesis: For task genres where model inferiority is asserted, median human performance under deployment-realistic conditions (time budgets, divided attention, fatigue) is substantially below the idealized reference, and models cross the realistic-human line earlier than the literature's narrative admits.
falsifiable_prediction: Measuring human cohorts under both idealized and realistic protocols on such genres will show large protocol-dependent performance gaps, with current models exceeding the realistic-condition human median on a subset of tasks where the idealized comparison still shows a model deficit.
why_important: Deployment decisions compare models to the humans who would actually do the job under real conditions; using idealized references delays beneficial automation and distorts risk analyses in both directions.
why_possibly_novel: Human-factors research measures realistic performance in other fields; importing dual-protocol human referencing into ML benchmark comparisons, with the model-crossing analysis, is hypothesized to be unpracticed (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pick 3 'humans are better' genres; run within-subject idealized vs realistic protocols; locate current model scores against both references.
main_risk: Defining 'realistic conditions' is domain-contentious; poorly justified realism choices would invite dismissal of the whole comparison.
community_default_belief: Humans comfortably outperform models on commonsense and everyday perception, so those comparisons need no measurement care.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The comfortable superiority may belong to idealized humans; measured humans under real constraints err at rates folk intuition does not predict.
fastest_falsification: If realistic and idealized human measurements coincide on these genres, the idealization critique is empty.

one_line: For deciding which of two models is better, crowd agreement panels reach the same verdicts as expert panels except on an identifiable minority stratum—so expertise can be budgeted, not defaulted.
problem: Human evaluation defaults to either cheap crowds (distrusted) or expensive experts (unscalable), with no evidence-based rule for when expert judgment actually changes the outcome.
core_hypothesis: On pairwise model-output comparisons, crowd-majority and expert-panel verdicts agree at rates indistinguishable from expert-expert agreement for most item types, with disagreement concentrated in a predictable stratum (specialized knowledge, subtle factuality) identifiable in advance from item features.
falsifiable_prediction: Parallel crowd and expert adjudication of the same comparison sets will show verdict-level equivalence overall (within pre-registered margins), item-feature models will predict the expert-necessary stratum with useful precision, and routing only that stratum to experts will recover full-expert conclusions at a fraction of cost.
why_important: Would replace ideological crowd-vs-expert debates with a routing rule, making rigorous human evaluation affordable at leaderboard scale.
why_possibly_novel: Crowd-expert agreement studies exist for labeling; the verdict-level equivalence claim for model comparison plus a validated expert-routing policy is hypothesized to be unbuilt (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect crowd and expert verdicts on ~1500 output pairs spanning genres; measure agreement against expert-expert baseline; train and validate the stratum router; test the routed protocol's fidelity.
main_risk: Expert-expert agreement itself may be low on subjective genres, making 'equivalence to experts' a weak and slippery reference.
community_default_belief: Trustworthy human evaluation of model outputs requires domain experts; crowd judgments are a compromise.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Most comparison verdicts hinge on qualities laypeople judge as reliably as experts; expertise binds only where specialized knowledge does.
fastest_falsification: If crowd-expert verdict agreement falls well below expert-expert agreement broadly rather than in a stratum, the routing premise fails.

one_line: Human-model agreement as a function of item ambiguity follows a stable two-parameter curve; items deviating from the curve flag ground truth that encodes annotator convention rather than task truth.
problem: Benchmarks contain items whose 'correct' labels reflect annotation-team conventions rather than facts about the task, but no scalable method separates convention-encoding items from genuine ones.
core_hypothesis: Plotting model-human agreement against independently measured item ambiguity yields a lawful curve for genuine items; items lying far below the curve (humans agree, models 'fail') are enriched for convention-encoded labels, and items far above it are enriched for label errors—turning curve residuals into an audit instrument.
falsifiable_prediction: Fitting the curve on multi-rater benchmarks and expert-auditing the outlier strata will confirm strong enrichment: below-curve outliers will be judged convention-encoded at rates far above baseline items, and above-curve outliers will be confirmed label errors at similarly elevated rates.
why_important: Provides an automatic triage separating three item populations (genuine, convention-encoded, mislabeled) that currently all count identically in scores and audits.
why_possibly_novel: Agreement statistics and label-error detection exist separately; the residual-from-ambiguity-curve construction as a convention detector is hypothesized to be new (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: On 2 multi-rater benchmarks, measure item ambiguity (rater entropy), compute model-human agreement per item across a zoo; fit the curve; expert-audit stratified samples of outliers vs on-curve items.
main_risk: Ambiguity measurement itself uses rater data, risking circularity; needs raters disjoint from those who produced the labels.
community_default_belief: When many humans agree on a label and models fail it, the models lack the capability the item tests.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Human agreement can reflect shared convention (learned guidelines) rather than task-intrinsic truth; models trained outside the convention fail the convention, not the task.
fastest_falsification: If outlier strata show no enrichment relative to on-curve items in expert audits, curve residuals carry no diagnostic content.

one_line: 'Human parity' is a frozen-test-set property: parity-achieving models fail on freshly collected same-task items where fresh human baselines hold steady, exposing parity as benchmark-specific.
problem: Parity announcements are read as task-level claims ('models now match humans at X'), but the evidence is a comparison on one aging test set that models' development ecosystems have long interacted with.
core_hypothesis: On freshly collected items matching the original task specification, parity-claiming models will fall measurably below their frozen-test performance while human baselines remain stable, showing that parity was achieved relative to a specific dataset rather than the task.
falsifiable_prediction: For benchmarks with historical parity claims, fresh same-spec collection will produce a significant model score drop paired with statistically stable human scores, and the model drop will exceed what distribution-shift metrics between old and new collections predict for capability-matched controls.
why_important: Parity claims anchor public and regulatory understanding of AI progress; showing they are dataset-indexed would impose fresh-data verification as a standard for such announcements.
why_possibly_novel: Fresh-test replications exist for accuracy; the asymmetric design using humans as a stability control to isolate model-specific parity decay is hypothesized to be unapplied (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select 3 parity-claim benchmarks; collect modest fresh same-spec test sets; measure both model and human performance on old and new sets; test the asymmetry (model drop, human stability).
main_risk: Fresh collections inevitably shift distribution; the human-stability control mitigates but cannot fully exclude content-drift explanations.
community_default_belief: Reaching human parity on the benchmark means the task is solved at human level.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The benchmark is one sample from the task, and years of community adaptation to that sample make model scores on it upward-biased in a way human scores are not.
fastest_falsification: If parity models hold their scores on fresh collections, parity was a task property after all.

one_line: Human baselines are unstable because protocols are, not because humans are: psychometrically corrected human references (lapse-rate modeling, attention screening) will replicate across labs.
problem: The variability of human baseline numbers across studies is cited as grounds for dismissing human references entirely, threatening the interpretability of all human-relative claims.
core_hypothesis: Most cross-study human baseline variance is attributable to protocol factors that psychophysics solved long ago (lapse rates, attention failures, instruction ambiguity); applying standard corrections yields human reference numbers that replicate across labs within tight tolerance.
falsifiable_prediction: A multi-site study running the same corrected protocol on the same benchmarks will produce between-lab baseline variance several times smaller than the variance among published uncorrected baselines for those benchmarks, with correction contributions decomposable per factor.
why_important: A replicable human reference restores meaning to human-relative evaluation, which otherwise degenerates into comparing models against measurement noise.
why_possibly_novel: Psychophysical rigor is standard in perception science; its systematic import to ML human-baseline methodology, with a multi-site replication demonstration, is hypothesized to be missing (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Standardize a corrected protocol (lapse modeling, catch trials, calibrated instructions); run it at 3 sites on 3 benchmarks; compare between-site variance to the published-baseline spread.
main_risk: Some benchmarks' tasks are so open-ended that psychophysical corrections don't apply, bounding the rehabilitation's scope.
community_default_belief: Human baselines are inherently soft numbers; between-study disagreement shows human references cannot anchor evaluation.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The disagreement tracks uncontrolled protocols, not intrinsic human variability; controlled psychophysics routinely achieves replicable human measurements.
fastest_falsification: If corrected protocols still yield large between-lab variance, human references are genuinely unstable and the rehabilitation fails.

one_line: A standardized 'human baseline protocol card' with measured sensitivity coefficients per protocol knob would make human references auditable; retrofitting it to popular benchmarks quantifies which knobs matter.
problem: Human baselines are reported as bare numbers without the protocol parameters (incentives, time, expertise, n, agreement) needed to interpret or compare them, and nobody knows which parameters matter how much.
core_hypothesis: Systematically varying protocol knobs in factorial human studies will yield stable sensitivity coefficients (score change per knob change) for each benchmark genre, enabling a protocol card standard that both documents baselines and permits approximate cross-protocol correction of legacy numbers.
falsifiable_prediction: Factorial protocol experiments will show consistent, genre-stable sensitivity coefficients for incentive level, time budget, and participant qualification, and corrections derived from them will reconcile a majority of discrepancies among published baselines for the same benchmarks.
why_important: Turns human baselines from unauditable folklore into documented measurements, and provides the correction table needed to salvage decades of legacy baseline numbers.
why_possibly_novel: Protocol effects are known qualitatively; measuring reusable sensitivity coefficients and standardizing a card that supports retroactive correction is hypothesized to be undeveloped (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run a fractional-factorial human study over 4 protocol knobs on 2 benchmarks from different genres; estimate coefficients; test reconciliation of published baseline discrepancies using the fitted corrections.
main_risk: Knob interactions (incentive x difficulty) may defeat additive correction, requiring larger designs than budgets allow.
community_default_belief: A human baseline is a fact about the task; how it was collected is a methods-section detail.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The baseline is a joint function of task and protocol; without the protocol coordinates, the number is uninterpretable and uncomparable.
fastest_falsification: If sensitivity coefficients vary wildly across replications within a genre, no stable correction table exists.

one_line: Committee-flagging plus human arbitration repairs test sets cheaply, and the repairs concentrate their ranking effects on near-tied model pairs—predictable in advance from gap statistics.
problem: Benchmark repair is treated as an all-or-nothing archival project, with no operational model of where repairs will actually change conclusions and hence where to spend arbitration effort.
core_hypothesis: Model-committee disagreement flags candidate label errors with high recall; human arbitration of flags yields repairs whose ranking impact concentrates on model pairs separated by less than the repair-induced score perturbation—a set enumerable beforehand from leaderboard gap statistics, making repair impact plannable.
falsifiable_prediction: On benchmarks with archived leaderboards, executing the flag-and-arbitrate pipeline will change outcomes only for pairs within the predicted gap band, with pairs outside the band unaffected, and the predicted-impact list will match realized changes with high precision.
why_important: Makes benchmark repair a scoped engineering task with forecastable consequences, lowering the activation energy for maintenance the field currently defers indefinitely.
why_possibly_novel: Label-error detection tools exist; the impact-forecasting layer (which conclusions will change, computed before repairing) as part of a repair methodology is hypothesized to be unbuilt (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run committee flagging on one benchmark; arbitrate a random half of flags; compare realized ranking changes to the gap-band forecast; verify the unarbitrated half predicts the same impact set.
main_risk: Committee flags inherit committee blind spots; recall against consensus errors is unknowable without independent full audit.
community_default_belief: Repairing a benchmark changes results unpredictably, so it is safer to leave known errors in place for comparability.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Repair effects are bounded arithmetic on score perturbations; their reach into rankings is computable, not mysterious.
fastest_falsification: If realized ranking changes appear outside the forecast gap band, impact is not predictable and the planning claim fails.

one_line: Repair ROI follows a steep decay law: the top few percent of disagreement-ranked items yield most ranking corrections, and the curve's shape is stable across benchmarks.
problem: Maintainers have no quantitative basis for sizing relabeling budgets: how much repair buys how much correction is unknown, so budgets are set by guesswork or not at all.
core_hypothesis: Ranking corrections as a function of relabel budget (items audited in committee-disagreement order) follow a sharply concave curve whose normalized shape is approximately benchmark-invariant, so a universal ROI curve fitted once predicts the marginal value of repair budgets on new benchmarks.
falsifiable_prediction: Replaying full audits on several benchmarks in disagreement order will produce normalized correction-vs-budget curves that collapse onto a common shape within tolerance, and the collapsed curve will predict the correction yield of a fresh benchmark's partial audit.
why_important: A stable ROI law converts benchmark maintenance from an unbounded obligation into a budgetable line item with known diminishing returns.
why_possibly_novel: Active-learning-style prioritization is familiar; the empirical claim of a cross-benchmark invariant ROI shape for evaluation repair, tested by curve collapse, is hypothesized to be new (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use 3 benchmarks with existing full audits; simulate ordered repair; normalize and overlay correction curves; test collapse and out-of-sample prediction on a fourth benchmark's partial audit.
main_risk: Benchmarks with systematically clustered errors (protocol-induced) may violate the collapse, splitting the law by error-generation mechanism.
community_default_belief: Meaningful benchmark cleaning requires auditing most of the dataset, so partial repair is not worth starting.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Errors that matter for rankings are concentrated where models disagree; the audit's value is front-loaded by construction.
fastest_falsification: If correction curves fail to collapse across the first three benchmarks, no universal ROI law exists.

one_line: Deleting suspect items is ranking-equivalent to relabeling them at matched budgets on most benchmarks, making cheap filtration the rational default repair policy.
problem: Repair debates assume relabeling (expensive, slow) is the gold standard and deletion (cheap, instant) is a lossy compromise, without measuring the decision-relevant difference between them.
core_hypothesis: For benchmarks of ordinary size and balance, deletion and expert relabeling of the same suspect-item set produce leaderboards whose disagreement is within resampling noise, because suspect items are few and their corrected labels distribute impact similarly to their absence; the equivalence breaks only for small or heavily imbalanced test sets where deletion distorts composition.
falsifiable_prediction: On benchmarks with completed relabel audits, re-scoring under deletion-of-flagged vs relabeled-flagged will show rank agreement at the bootstrap ceiling for adequately sized balanced benchmarks, with divergence appearing as test size shrinks or class skew grows, matching the predicted breakdown boundary.
why_important: If deletion suffices, benchmark repair becomes an afternoon's work instead of a funded project, removing the chief practical excuse for leaving known errors in place.
why_possibly_novel: Both repair modes are used ad hoc; the head-to-head equivalence test with a characterized breakdown boundary as a policy rule is hypothesized to be unrun (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 3 audited benchmarks, construct deletion and relabel variants; re-score public models; test rank equivalence; repeat on subsampled/skewed versions to locate the breakdown boundary.
main_risk: Flagged-item sets from audits may under-represent systematic errors whose deletion and relabeling genuinely differ, understating divergence.
community_default_belief: Proper benchmark repair means fixing labels; deleting problem items sacrifices validity for convenience.
why_that_may_be_wrong: For ranking purposes, removing noise and correcting noise are nearly the same operation unless the removed mass is large or skewed; validity intuitions imported from training data do not apply to evaluation.
fastest_falsification: Material rank disagreement between deletion and relabel variants on a large balanced benchmark kills the equivalence.

one_line: Committee-based repair embeds the current model generation's priors: consensus blind spots become permanently unfixable, and repaired benchmarks drift toward grading similarity-to-committee.
problem: Model committees are becoming the standard tool for finding label errors, but items where all committee members share the same wrong belief are structurally invisible to the method, and repeated committee-based repair may bias benchmarks toward the committee's family.
core_hypothesis: Committee-repaired benchmarks acquire a measurable bias: post-repair, models similar to the repair committee gain score relative to dissimilar models beyond what independent human-only repair produces, and injected consensus-error items (all committee members wrong identically) survive repair at near-100% rates.
falsifiable_prediction: A controlled comparison of committee-guided vs human-only repair on the same benchmark will show family-similarity score gains specific to the committee-guided variant, and seeded consensus errors will evade committee flagging while random-error seeds are caught at high rates.
why_important: The field is about to institutionalize model-in-the-loop benchmark maintenance; documenting its structural blind spot and bias direction before it becomes universal would shape safer repair protocols (committee diversity requirements, human-only audit strata).
why_possibly_novel: Model-assisted cleaning is celebrated for recall; its selection bias on the surviving benchmark and the unfixability of consensus errors are hypothesized to be uncharacterized (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Seed a benchmark copy with consensus-error and random-error items (constructed via committee-blind adversarial search); run committee repair; measure differential detection rates and post-repair family-similarity score shifts against a human-only repair arm.
main_risk: Constructing genuine consensus errors requires finding inputs where diverse models fail identically, which may be hard enough to weaken the seeding methodology.
community_default_belief: Model committees find label errors more thoroughly and objectively than human auditing, so committee-based cleaning strictly improves benchmarks.
why_that_may_be_wrong: A committee can only see errors it disagrees about; its shared priors define a class of errors it certifies as truth, and each repair round transfers those priors into the benchmark.
fastest_falsification: If seeded consensus errors are caught at rates comparable to random errors, the blind-spot mechanism is not operating.

one_line: A monthly trickle of fresh human-verified items through a leaderboard—a benchmark 'immune system'—detects overfitting drift as static-vs-fresh score divergence with known alarm statistics.
problem: Benchmark corruption (overfitting, contamination, drift) is discovered years late via one-off replication studies; no benchmark operates a continuous integrity monitor.
core_hypothesis: Routing a small monthly stream of freshly authored, human-verified items (matched to the static set's difficulty profile via calibration) alongside the static test set yields a divergence statistic whose null distribution is estimable from replicate noise, enabling timely, statistically controlled alarms for benchmark corruption.
falsifiable_prediction: In retrospective simulation (replaying leaderboards with reconstructed fresh streams) and one live deployment, the monitor will flag known corruption events (documented contamination or overfitting episodes) within a few cycles at controlled false-alarm rates, where static-only monitoring detects nothing.
why_important: Moves benchmark integrity from archaeology to operations: corruption gets caught while the leaderboard still matters, protecting the decisions being made on it.
why_possibly_novel: Fresh test sets and monitoring exist separately; the calibrated-stream design with formal alarm statistics as permanent benchmark infrastructure is hypothesized to be unimplemented (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build the difficulty-matched stream protocol for one active leaderboard; run it for several cycles; validate alarm calibration on injected synthetic corruption (models fine-tuned on static items) and measure detection latency.
main_risk: Sustained fresh-item authorship at matched difficulty is an ongoing cost and itself drifts; the monitor needs monitoring.
community_default_belief: Benchmark validity is checked, if ever, by occasional replication studies after suspicion arises.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Corruption is a continuous process with a detectable signature; waiting for suspicion guarantees detection lags damage by years.
fastest_falsification: If the monitor cannot detect even deliberate static-set fine-tuning in live deployment, the divergence statistic lacks power.

one_line: Error-aware rescoring (scoring against label posteriors instead of hard labels) rehabilitates 'broken' benchmarks: most historical conclusions stand once label uncertainty is priced in.
problem: High-profile label-error findings have led to blanket distrust of affected benchmarks and the conclusions drawn on them, but hard-label scoring was the fragile element, not necessarily the data or the conclusions.
core_hypothesis: Replacing hard labels with label posteriors (estimated from audits and rater models) yields rescored leaderboards that preserve the large majority of historical comparative conclusions on 'broken' benchmarks, localizing genuine damage to a small identifiable set of comparisons rather than the benchmark wholesale.
falsifiable_prediction: Posterior-based rescoring of benchmarks with published error audits will reproduce historical rankings above the bootstrap ceiling for most model pairs, with the changed conclusions concentrated among pairs whose gaps were below the label-noise floor—quantifying exactly which literature claims need revision.
why_important: Prevents wasteful wholesale abandonment of benchmark infrastructure and historical knowledge, replacing 'benchmark X is broken' with a precise list of which conclusions on X were and were not sound.
why_possibly_novel: Label-error audits and probabilistic labels both exist; using posterior rescoring specifically as a rehabilitation instrument that adjudicates historical conclusions is hypothesized to be unattempted (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 2 audited benchmarks, construct label posteriors from audit data; rescore archived submissions; enumerate preserved vs overturned pairwise conclusions and their relation to the noise floor.
main_risk: Posterior construction from partial audits requires extrapolation assumptions that critics can dispute, softening the rehabilitation's authority.
community_default_belief: Benchmarks shown to contain widespread label errors are broken, and results reported on them are unreliable.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Errors known and modeled are just measurement uncertainty; conclusions robust to that uncertainty were never actually threatened by the errors' existence.
fastest_falsification: If posterior rescoring overturns historical conclusions broadly rather than only near the noise floor, the damage was real and wholesale distrust justified.

one_line: Anchored equating can place all forks of a fragmented benchmark family (cleaned variants, subsets, re-releases) on one comparable scale, ending fork-induced incomparability.
problem: Popular benchmarks fragment into forks (cleaned versions, filtered subsets, re-annotations), and results across forks are silently incomparable, fracturing the literature's evidence base.
core_hypothesis: Because forks share substantial item overlap, standard anchor-based equating can map all fork scores onto a common scale with quantifiable error, and applying the mapping retroactively will reconcile a large share of apparently conflicting cross-fork results in the literature.
falsifiable_prediction: Equating transforms fitted on shared items will predict models' scores across forks within stated error bars, and a survey of cross-fork 'contradictions' in published results will show most dissolving under the common scale, with the irreducible remainder flagging genuine fork-semantic differences.
why_important: Restores comparability across a fragmented evidence base without asking anyone to re-run experiments, and provides fork authors a standard for maintaining comparability by design.
why_possibly_novel: Equating is standard psychometrics; its application to reconcile ML benchmark fork families and audit literature contradictions is hypothesized to be unpracticed (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take one benchmark family with 3+ forks; fit anchor equating on overlap items using a shared model zoo; validate cross-fork score prediction on held-out models; re-examine a sample of published cross-fork discrepancies under the mapping.
main_risk: Forks differ precisely on contested items (that is why they forked); anchor items may be unrepresentative of fork-divergent content, biasing the transform.
community_default_belief: Once a benchmark forks, results on different forks are simply different experiments; comparability is lost.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Forks are overlapping measurements of one construct; shared items carry enough information to calibrate the offset between them.
fastest_falsification: If equated cross-fork predictions miss held-out models' scores beyond stated error, fork semantics dominate and the common scale is fiction.

one_line: Sealed replicate test sets escrowed at release with a trusted third party turn contamination disputes into decidable measurements: the sealed-vs-public gap at opening quantifies cumulative corruption.
problem: Contamination and overfitting accusations against benchmarks are undecidable after the fact because no uncorrupted reference measurement exists once the test set has circulated.
core_hypothesis: Collecting a same-protocol replicate test set at release time, sealing it (hash-committed, third-party escrowed), and opening it at a pre-committed trigger provides an unbiased corruption estimator: the score gap between public and sealed sets for contemporary models, measured with known statistical properties because both sets predate all disputes.
falsifiable_prediction: For pilot benchmarks operating the escrow protocol, opening events will produce gap measurements with confidence intervals tight enough to adjudicate corruption claims (gap indistinguishable from zero, or significantly positive), and retrospective simulation on replicated legacy benchmarks will show the estimator correctly ranking benchmarks by independently documented corruption levels.
why_important: Converts the most corrosive recurring dispute in evaluation—'is this benchmark still valid?'—from rhetoric into a measurement with pre-registered decision rules, at the modest cost of collecting the test set twice.
why_possibly_novel: Private test sets and hash commitments exist separately; the sealed-replicate design specifically as a future-proof corruption adjudicator with pre-committed opening triggers is hypothesized to be unimplemented (not literature-verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Launch the protocol on one new benchmark (public plus sealed replicate); simultaneously run a retrospective validation using an existing benchmark with a known replicate collection; verify the estimator's error bars and its agreement with documented corruption history.
main_risk: The sealed set ages with the world (topical drift), so late openings conflate corruption with drift; the design needs a drift-control arm (fresh items collected at opening) to separate them.
community_default_belief: Once a benchmark has been public for years, there is no way to establish definitively whether its scores remain trustworthy.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Trustworthiness is only unmeasurable because the reference measurement was never banked; a sealed twin collected at birth makes the question empirical forever after.
fastest_falsification: If the retrospective estimator fails to rank known-corruption benchmarks correctly, the sealed-gap statistic does not measure corruption.
